Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Gerbil = Mongolian jird - Meriones unguiculatus
UT.note: Listed under 'Domestic mammals and mammalian livestock not covered under this rule', so R657-3b does not reach it and no certificate of registration arises.

PA.quote: Unless otherwise provided in this section or the act, it is unlawful for a person to import, possess, sell, offer for sale or release within this Commonwealth the following wild animals or wild birds or the eggs of the birds or a crossbreed or hybrid of the wild animals or wild birds, which are similar in appearance
PA.note: The Mongolian gerbil appears in none of the eleven categories the Game Commission prohibits, which run to cats, canids, bears, raccoons, nutria, skunks, primates, listed species, the monk parakeet, and wildlife taken from the wild or captive bred out of state. Read literally, § 137.1(a)(11) bars possessing any wildlife captive bred in another state, and 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines wild animals as every mammal except horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs, so the text reaches far wider than the Game Commission applies it. The Commission draws its line at undomesticated species, which is why hedgehogs and sugar gliders are pursued and long domesticated pets are not.

CA.quote: Family Psittacidae-Parrots, Parakeets: Myiopsitta monachus (Monk or Quaker parakeet) (D)

GA.note: Absent from the bird list.

NYC.note: Bird entry covers predatory or large birds only. NY State is a separate question.

NJ.note: Not among the nine exempt birds.

ME.note: Expressly carved out of the unrestricted list: 'Except for: Myiopsitta monachus'.

CO.note: Colorado clears the whole parrot group on its unregulated wildlife list without carving out the monk parakeet, which most states that mention the species do.

VA.quote: Exception for certain monk parakeets. No permit is required for monk parakeets (quakers) that have been captive bred and are closed-banded with a seamless band.
VA.note: Virginia lists Myiopsitta monachus in the subsection A permit table and then writes an exception for the birds people actually buy. A captive bred quaker wearing a seamless closed band needs no permit. A wild caught bird, or one with an open band that could have been fitted later, does. The band is the whole test, so keep the paperwork that came with the bird.

grandfathered.detail: An asterisked animal held before 1 July 1992 could be kept if declared to the department in writing by 1 January 1993. That declaration works as a possession-only permit, renews every five years and cannot be transferred.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians, non-poultry birds, hedgehogs, tenrecs, and sugar gliders
ID.note: The only bird on the deleterious exotic animal list is the mute swan.

KY.quote: Monk or Quaker parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus);
KY.note: The permit-exempt list confirms the exclusion: it clears parrots, lovebirds, budgerigars, macaws and parakeets except the monk parakeet.

RI.quote: Psittacidae (Parrots and their allies) except for Myiopsitta monachus (Monk Parakeet), which requires a permit,

NH.quote: Parrots (Psittaciformes);
NH.note: Listed by order rather than species, and no monk parakeet exception appears anywhere in Fis 800.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds (including ring-necked pheasants and gray partridge) native to the continental United States
MO.note: Myiopsitta monachus is South American. Naturalised colonies exist in the United States but the species is not native to it.

SC.quote: 6. shell parakeets 7. love birds 8. cockatiels 9. parrots
SC.note: The only bird needing a permit under § 50-16-20 is turkey of the genus Meleagris. South Carolina makes no monk parakeet exception, unlike most states that name the species.

MT.quote: Psittacidae (parrots)
MT.note: Montana clears the whole parrot family on its statutory noncontrolled list and makes no monk parakeet exception, which most states do.

WV.quote: The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No bird category appears in the guidance at all.

AK.quote: Parrot, parakeet, cockatiel, macaw, and other members of the Family Psittacidae not prohibited by federal or international law
AK.note: The family is cleared as a whole with no monk parakeet exception, which is unusual.

AL.note: The only bird restrictions in the rule are wild turkey strains and anything federally listed as injurious. The monk parakeet is neither.

IN.note: No bird appears on any of the three class lists.

ND.note: No bird restriction appears in the chapter. The only bird provision is a seven dollar annual licence fee for bird species that the board requires to be licensed.

WY.quote: a permit shall not be issued for importation or possession of the following live warm-blooded wildlife in Wyoming... (iii) Monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus);
WY.note: Not merely unpermitted. The regulation says a permit shall not be issued, which closes the route entirely.

MS.note: No bird appears on the list.

LA.note: The regulation reaches wild quadrupeds, big exotic cats and non-human primates. No bird is listed.

OK.quote: The following list of birds shall be exempt from import and export requirements... (2) Psittacine birds (parrots, parakeets and budgerigars).
OK.note: Cleared by group with no monk parakeet exception.

NE.quote: Cage and Aviary Birds - Means those captive-reared birds, not native to Nebraska, such as parrots, exotic finches, and canaries, which are adapted to live and breed in a cage. For purposes of this regulation, the monk parakeet (Myiopsitta monachus) is not a cage and aviary bird.
NE.note: A neat piece of drafting to watch for. The importation list ends with All Cage and Aviary Birds, and the definitions section removes the monk parakeet from that category by name, so the one bird excluded from the definition is the one bird that cannot be imported.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No bird is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Your county code is the operative layer.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No bird appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: Nondomestic birds are handled by ARSD 12:68:13 rather than the mammal permit list here.

DC.quote: Captive-bred species of common cage birds, including chickens
DC.note: A monk parakeet is a common cage bird and captive bred, so it clears the bird category. DC is one of the few places that does not single the species out.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: The bird list runs to dozens of parrots by name and the monk parakeet is not among them, so it stays inside Code 09.02 rather than being exempted. This is the usual pattern: the monk parakeet is the one parrot states single out, because established colonies damage electrical infrastructure.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: No bird of any kind is on the dangerous wild animal list, and Ohio has no separate monk parakeet provision, so the species is unrestricted here while most states single it out.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: No bird is a potentially dangerous wild animal, and the only bird on the deleterious exotic wildlife rule is the mute swan. Washington is one of the states where the monk parakeet is simply unregulated.

WI.quote: Monk or Quaker parakeet or parrot (Myiopsitta monachus) - Prohibited
WI.note: The one psittacine Wisconsin prohibits. NR 40 Prohibited status bars possession, transport and transfer without a permit, so this is the rare case where the parrot order's general clearance as an unregulated pet bird does not apply.

UT.quote: Parrots - Family Psittacidae - All species not native to North America
UT.note: Utah clears the whole parrot family by one line, provided the species is not native to North America. Unlike Wisconsin and a number of other states, Utah draws no monk parakeet carve-out, so the Quaker sits in the same noncontrolled column as the African grey and the cockatoo.

PA.quote: The Monk Parakeet, Myiopsitts monachus , sometimes referred to as the Quaker Parakeet or Gray-headed Parakeet.
PA.note: Named outright, which makes this one of the few Pennsylvania exotic pet answers that needs no interpretation at all: import, possession, sale, offering for sale and release are each unlawful. The scientific name is misspelled in the official text, which prints Myiopsitts for Myiopsitta. This is the only parrot Pennsylvania designates, and the designation is what brings the species inside the Game Code, since 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 otherwise limits wild birds to federally listed migratory birds and game birds.

MI.quote: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is required for the import of exotic, circus and zoo animals, native wild animals, domestic rabbits, nonnative rodents, nonnative reptiles and amphibians, and non-poultry birds
MI.note: The monk or quaker parakeet is named in no Michigan statute or order. The Large Carnivore Act covers cats and bears, the captive game permit covers native game, and the herp order covers reptiles and amphibians, so nothing reaches a pet parrot. The only requirement is the certificate of veterinary inspection for a non-poultry bird moved into the state. Worth checking against your own state, because Michigan does not follow Pennsylvania, which bans this species by name.

CA.quote: Domestic cats and hybrids of domestic cats are not restricted

DC.quote: Domestic cats, excluding hybrids with ocelots or margays
DC.note: The Bengal derives from the Asian leopard cat, which is neither.

NYC.quote: All cats other than domesticated cats (Felis catus), including ... any hybrid offspring of a wild cat and domesticated cat.

NY.note: Felidae hybrids are wild animals except registered hybrids with no wild felid ancestry for five or more generations, so an F5 or later Bengal qualifies. NYC bans all wild-cat hybrids regardless.

MN.note: The definition expressly reaches 'any hybrid or cross between an animal listed as prohibited and a domestic animal and offspring from all subsequent generations', so unlike New York there is no generation at which a Bengal falls out.

MD.quote: hybrid of a member of the cat family and a domestic cat if the hybrid weighs over 30 pounds
MD.note: Maryland draws the line by weight rather than by generation. A Bengal under 30 lb is outside the prohibition, which most Bengals are.

ID.quote: Geoffroy's Cat (Felis geoffroyi). Margay (Felis wiedii). Ocelot (Felis pardalis). Serval (Felis serval).
ID.note: The small felidae list is these four. The Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal, Prionailurus bengalensis, is not on it, and cats are conventional pets under IDAPA 13.01.10.

IA.quote: The bengal must be the fourth or later filial generation of offspring with the first filial generation being the offspring of a domestic cat and an Asian leopard cat, and each subsequent generation being the offspring of a domestic cat.
IA.note: F4 and later are carved out of the definition. F1 to F3 are dangerous wild animals and are banned.

KY.quote: Lions, jaguars, leopards, or tigers (Genus Panthera); Lynx (Genus Lynx);
KY.note: Prionailurus bengalensis appears on neither list, and the hybrid clause in Section 4(2)(v) reaches only hybrids of species in that subsection.

RI.quote: Domestic Cat (Felis catus) excluding hybrids with wild felines,
RI.note: An F1 cross is plainly excluded from the domestic animal list and then caught by the § 3.9(B) bar on permits for Carnivora hybrids. A late generation Bengal is the offspring of two domestic cats, so on the § 3.6(A)(13) definition of hybrid it arguably is not one. The regulation sets no filial generation cut off the way Iowa and New York do. Ask the Division of Agriculture before buying.

NH.quote: 5   Tiger; Golden Tabby, Siberian, White Siberian, Bengal   Panthera tigeris
NH.note: The only Bengal in the controlled table is the tiger colour morph. Neither Prionailurus bengalensis nor domestic cat hybrids appear, and domestic cats are not wildlife under these rules.

MO.quote: any lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, Canada lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi
MO.note: The statute names species and says nothing about hybrids or filial generations.

KS.quote: Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof;
KS.note: The hybrid clause attaches to those six species. Leopard here means Panthera pardus, not the Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal.

SC.quote: Family Felidae, Genus panthera—all lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cougars, cheetahs, snow leopards, and clouded leopards;
SC.note: The hybrid clause in § 47-2-10(2) attaches to those animals. The Asian leopard cat is Prionailurus, not Panthera.

MT.quote: The term includes livestock, as defined in 81-2-702, dogs, cats, rodents, Eurasian ferrets, and poultry.
MT.note: Cats are domestic animals under the definition, and nothing in the exotic wildlife lists mentions the Asian leopard cat or its hybrids.

WV.quote: "Domestic animal" means an animal which, through extremely long association with humans, has been bred to a degree which has resulted in genetic changes affecting the temperament, color, conformation or other attributes of the species to an extent that makes it unique and distinguishable from a wild individual of its species, and includes an animal that has been bred as a companion animal.
WV.note: Domestic animals are excluded from the definition of a dangerous wild animal. A registered Bengal is bred as a companion animal.

AK.quote: The following species, not including a hybrid of a game animal and a species listed in this subsection, may be possessed, imported, exported, bought, sold, or traded without a permit
AK.note: Cat, Felis catus, is on the clean list but hybrids of a listed species and a game animal are carved straight back out, and subsection (c) then bars any pet permit for such a hybrid by name. The rule sets no filial generation cut off, so it gives no comfort to a late generation Bengal the way Iowa and New York do.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The words or any of its hybrids sit in the operative sentence rather than in a separate clause, so a Bengal is caught by the Felidae entry. No filial generation cut off is given.

AL.quote: black bear (Ursus americanus), mountain lion (Felis concolor), bobcat (Felis rufus)
AL.note: No hybrid clause appears anywhere in the rule.

IN.quote: (12) Leopard cat (Prionailurus bengalensis)... A hybrid of any of these species with a domestic dog or domestic cat is exempt from permitting under this section.
IN.note: Indiana answers the Bengal question outright. The leopard cat itself needs a Class II permit, and its hybrid with a domestic cat is exempt by name, with no filial generation condition attached.

ND.quote: "Domestic animal" means dog, cat, horse, bovine animal, sheep, goat, bison, farmed elk, llama, alpaca, or swine.
ND.note: Cats are domestic animals under the statute and no hybrid clause appears anywhere in the chapter.

WY.quote: "Domestic Animals" means those populations of animals, their viable gametes (eggs and sperm), fertilized eggs, or any hybrid or transgenic product thereof, which through long association with humans have been bred to a degree which has resulted in genetic changes of the species to an extent that makes them unique and distinguishable from wild individuals of their species. For the purpose of this regulation, only the following animals are considered domestic: ...cat (Felis catus),
WY.note: The definition folds hybrids into the domestic category rather than carving them out, which is the opposite of how Rhode Island and Alaska handle the same question.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: Prionailurus is not named, and the only hybrid clause in the rule is the one for wolf crosses under Canidae.

LA.quote: vii. all subspecies of the above listed exotic cats; viii. hybrids resulting from cross breeding of the above listed exotic cats.
LA.note: The Asian leopard cat is not one of the six listed cats, so a Bengal is outside the hybrid clause.

OK.quote: (4) Cats (except native cats and bears).

NE.note: The only cats in the chapter are Nebraska's two native ones, and both are marked for commercial purposes only. A domestic cat is not a wild mammal.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

VA.quote: Felidae   All Species   Cats*
VA.note: The table restricts the cat family without exception and without a hybrid clause, which is the problem. A Bengal is registered as Felis catus but carries leopard cat ancestry, and the rule offers no filial generation line to settle which side it falls. Ask the Department of Wildlife Resources before buying.

HI.quote: Felis catus crossed with lynx, ocelot, margay, puma, jaguarandi, bobcat, leopard cat, wild cat, etc. ... cat, hybrid; (all hybrid-crosses where one or both parents are prohibited or restricted)
HI.note: Hawaii is one of the few states to write the hybrid question into the rule instead of leaving it open. The prohibited list names the leopard cat cross specifically, and § 150A-6.2(b) sets up an expert committee to settle disputed lineage. There is no filial generation cutoff, so a late generation Bengal is in the same position as an F1.

ME.quote: Carnivora (Carnivores)   Mustela putorius furo   Domestic Ferret
ME.note: A Bengal is registered as Felis catus, and a domestic cat is not wildlife, so the unrestricted list is arguably the wrong document to consult. But the list clears exactly one carnivore, and Maine regulates hybrids of wild species elsewhere in its wildlife rules. Nothing here settles which side a Bengal falls on. Ask Inland Fisheries and Wildlife before buying.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: The unrestricted list names one hybrid, the wolf and dog cross, and no cat of any kind. A Bengal is registered as a domestic cat, so whether Code 09.02 reaches it at all is the question, and this document does not answer it. Ask the Game and Fish Commission.

OH.quote: All of the following, including hybrids with domestic cats unless otherwise specified: (a) Cheetahs; (b) Lynxes ... (c) Cougars ... (d) Caracals; (e) Servals, excluding hybrids with domestic cats commonly known as savannah cats.
OH.note: Ohio is unusually clear about cat hybrids, and the Asian leopard cat is not on the dangerous wild animal list in any form. The five cats whose hybrids are caught are named, and Prionailurus is not among them, so a Bengal is an ordinary domestic cat here. Ohio even carves the savannah cat out expressly, which shows the drafters had hybrids in mind.

WA.quote: Family felidae, only lions, tigers, captive-bred cougars, jaguars, cheetahs, leopards, snow leopards, and clouded leopards
WA.note: The word only is doing the work. Washington names eight big cats and reaches their hybrids, but Prionailurus bengalensis is not among them, so a Bengal falls outside the statute no matter what filial generation it is.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Cat - Felis catus - including breeds that are recognized by The International Cat Association as Preliminary New, Advanced New, Non-championship, and Championship Breeds
UT.note: Utah resolves cat hybrids by TICA recognition rather than by generation, and the Bengal is a TICA Championship breed, so it lands in the domestic column outside the rule. That is an unusually clean answer next to the generation tests used by New York and Iowa.

PA.quote: In the family Felidae . Species and subspecies, except species which are commonly called house cats which may be possessed but not released into the wild.
PA.note: Genuinely unresolved, and the ambiguity is structural. The Bengal is a cross between the domestic cat and the Asian leopard cat, so it sits on both sides of this line at once: the opening sentence of § 137.1(a) prohibits a crossbreed or hybrid of the listed animals which are similar in appearance, while the Felidae line exempts species commonly called house cats. Nothing in the regulation names a filial generation, a percentage of wild ancestry, or the Bengal itself, so an early generation animal and a late generation one get the same silent text. Rendered grey rather than guessed.

MI.quote: any of the following cats of the Felidae family, whether wild or captive bred, including a hybrid cross with such a cat: a lion, a leopard (including a snow leopard or clouded leopard), a jaguar, a tiger, a cougar, a panther, or a cheetah
MI.note: The Large Carnivore Act runs on a closed list, and the drafters showed how they expand it: they wrote leopard and then spelled out that snow leopards and clouded leopards count. The Asian leopard cat behind the Bengal is Prionailurus bengalensis, a small Asian cat that is not a leopard and is not one of the animals they chose to name. The hybrid clause reaches a cross with such a cat, meaning one of the listed seven, so it does not catch this cross either. Nothing else in Michigan names domestic cat hybrids.

CA.note: The reptile list covers crocodilians, snapping turtles, venomous snakes and the Gila monster only.

GA.note: Reptile list names two pythons, the Argentine tegu and the Nile monitor only.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles
DC.note: Lizards are absent from the permitted list entirely.

NYC.note: Chamaeleonidae absent from the reptile entry.

NJ.quote: any other exotic species not exempted
NJ.note: New Jersey exempts a closed list of species from permitting and then requires a permit for anything else. The veiled chameleon is not exempted, so a personal possession permit from Fish and Wildlife applies before the animal arrives.

ME.note: Named by binomial on the unrestricted list, so no permit of any kind applies.

FL.note: Not on the prohibited list.

NY.note: New York's wild animal definition is closed by those five words. Among reptiles it reaches venomous species, named large pythons and monitors, and crocodilians. A chameleon is none of those. Note that New York City bans separately and more broadly.

CT.quote: The felidae... the canidae... the ursidae... and the hominidae
CT.note: The list is entirely mammalian. Connecticut restricts no reptile under this section.

MA.note: Except species categorically nonexempt under endangered species protections.

CO.quote: All non-native tropical and subtropical species of lizards ... Chamaeleonidae (chameleons)

OR.note: Oregon's exotic animal definition is closed: non-indigenous cats other than the domestic cat, non-human primates, non-wolf non-indigenous canids other than the domestic dog, bears other than the black bear, and crocodilians. The only reptiles in it are crocodilians.

WA.note: Varanidae covers water and crocodile monitors only; no chameleons.

OH.note: The only lizard listed is the Komodo dragon.

VA.note: Chamaeleonidae is absent from the permit table.

AR.quote: Veiled Chameleon (Chamaeleo calyptratus)
AR.cite: Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.note: Named individually on the unrestricted list, so no permit is required.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

KY.note: The only lizards restricted are gila monsters and beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, and nothing else.

RI.quote: Old World Chameleons (Chameleonidae) may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;

MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so outside Class I, and not a deadly or dangerous reptile.

KS.note: Only snakes are named among the reptiles, and only venomous ones.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous lizards not on the controlled or prohibited lists, including but not limited to the following families or subfamilies: ...(vi) Chamaeleonidae (chameleons);

WV.quote: The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: The only reptiles in the guidance are large constrictors, venomous snakes and crocodilians.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AL.note: Only tegus of the genus Salvator are named among the lizards.

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or in the current administrative rules.

WY.quote: (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

LA.note: On neither the prohibited nor the restricted nonnative list. The restricted lizards are the Asian water monitor, brown basilisk, spiny-tailed iguana, curly-tailed lizard and Peter's rock agama.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license

HI.quote: The introduction into Hawaii of live animals or live non-domestic animals as defined in this chapter at any stage of development is prohibited except for those animals on the lists
HI.note: Chamaeleo calyptratus appears on no Hawaii list. The only chameleons named anywhere are Chamaeleo chamaeleon and Furcifer oustaleti, both on the restricted list for research and exhibition only. Veiled chameleons are established in the wild on Maui and Oahu, which is exactly the outcome the default rule exists to prevent.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: varanidae limited to water and crocodile monitors, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. Nothing here is among them.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The veiled chameleon is native to the Arabian Peninsula and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The veiled chameleon is an Arabian species and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

CA.note: Only Chelydridae among turtles.

GA.note: Testudines list names only Pelomedusa subrufa and Pelodiscus sinensis.

DC.note: Statute says 'turtles'; a tortoise is Testudines, so this is defensible rather than express.

NYC.note: The city bans all members of Chelydridae, the snapping turtles, and turtles under four inches, but no tortoise. Testudo horsfieldii is outside the prohibition.

NJ.quote: any other exotic species not exempted
NJ.note: Not on the exempt list, so the catch-all permit provision applies. This is the only permit requirement for a Russian tortoise anywhere in the country.

ME.note: Maine's list mislabels it 'Greek Tortoise'. The binomial is Horsfield's/Russian; Greek is T. graeca.

NY.note: No tortoise appears in the closed definition, which among reptiles covers venomous species, named large pythons and monitors, and crocodilians.

AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: The unrestricted list has no invertebrate section, so whether a tarantula needs an exemption depends on whether the Game and Fish Commission's definition of wildlife reaches invertebrates at all. Most state game codes stop at vertebrates, but Arkansas's does list mussels among the aquatic wildlife it regulates, which cuts the other way.

CA.quote: (8) Class Crustacea   Crustaceans ... (9) Class Gastropoda   Slugs, Snails ... (10) Class Bivalvia   Bivalves
CA.note: Section 671 reaches invertebrates, but only three classes of them: crustaceans, gastropods and bivalves, all aquatic or agricultural concerns. No arachnid appears anywhere in the manual.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Chapter 935 lists no invertebrate. The only match for the word spider in the statute is the black spider monkey, which is a primate.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: The statute covers mammals and reptiles only, so no invertebrate is reached.

WI.cite: Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 40; Wis. Stat. § 169.04(4)(b)
WI.note: No invertebrate kept as a pet appears on NR 40, whose terrestrial invertebrate entries are forest and soil pests such as the emerald ash borer and jumping worm. Non-native species are outside captive wildlife licensing.

PA.quote: Wild birds, wild mammals and facsimiles thereof, regardless of classification, whether protected or unprotected, including any part, product, egg or offspring thereof, or the dead body or parts thereof (excluding fossils), whether or not included in a manufactured product or in a processed food product.
PA.note: A tarantula is neither a bird nor a mammal, so it is not wildlife and the Game Commission has no authority over it. The Fish and Boat Commission's Chapter 79 covers reptiles and amphibians. Pennsylvania's two animal agencies divide the field between them and a terrestrial invertebrate falls in the gap, so no state possession rule applies.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: A tarantula is not a reptile or amphibian, so the herp order does not reach it, and it is not a cat, a bear or native game, so neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the captive game permit reaches it either. Michigan regulates terrestrial invertebrates through its invasive species list rather than any pet law, and no common pet invertebrate is on it.

RI.quote: Nothing in this Part shall prohibit any person from possession of exotic animals or native animals of the class Insecta unless the animals of that class appear on the list of prohibited insects
RI.note: Same gap as the tarantula. Scorpions are arachnids, not insects.

MT.quote: Emperor scorpion - Pandinus imperator;
MT.note: Named individually, along with the Tanzanian redclaw. Those two are the entire arachnid list.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess... any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following
DC.note: No invertebrate category exists in the permitted list.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian. No invertebrate appears in it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: The permit provision at § 50-16-20 lists furbearers, cervids, pigs, peccaries, bovids, coyote, bear and turkey. No invertebrate is in it, and Chapter 47-2 covers only big cats, bears and great apes.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No invertebrate appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.

WV.note: No invertebrate appears in the categories the board is directed to consider.

IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No invertebrate appears.

NE.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person or persons to retain any wild birds or wild mammals (as defined in Nebraska revised statute 37-245 and 37-246) in captivity except the following species may be kept under authority of a Captive Wildlife Permit
NE.note: Cynomys is a Nebraska wild mammal and is absent from the list that follows, which runs from badger to long-tailed weasel. It is also absent from the importation list.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: Not one of the six named cats or a bear, so outside the only exotic pet statute Kansas has.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: Not a bear, big cat, canid or primate, which with large snakes and crocodilians is the whole of the guidance.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: Not in the orders the possession permit list names, which are Carnivora in five families, Artiodactyla, two Perissodactyla families, Proboscidea and Primates.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: No rodent is in the dangerous wild animal definition. Chapter 481A names the Sciuridae as game only in the sense of gray and fox squirrels.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: Cynomys is on no Hawaii list, so the default prohibition applies.

MT.quote: "Exotic wildlife" means a wildlife species that is not native to Montana.
MT.note: Both the black-tailed and white-tailed prairie dog are native, so the exotic wildlife white list does not apply, and Montana's only prairie dog rules are the translocation program at ARM 12.9.1001 through 12.9.1035, which governs moving whole colonies between wild sites under department approval and plague monitoring. Nothing there addresses keeping one as a pet in either direction.

ME.note: The unrestricted rodent list runs to thirteen species, all of them small cage animals. Cynomys is not among them.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: No Cynomys is on the unrestricted mammal list, so the restriction and permit codes still apply.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Except as otherwise listed, all species are presumed prohibited. All species not listed will require an assessment before collection, importation, or possession will be authorized.
UT.note: Not listed anywhere in Table 3b-1, and the table's default is inverted: unlisted birds and mammals are 'presumed prohibited' and require a division assessment before possession will be authorized. So this is neither cleared nor expressly banned, it is an application to DWR with no published answer. Utah also has its own native species, the federally threatened Utah prairie dog, which is protected separately from anything in this table.

PA.quote: Game or wild held captive . Game or wildlife held in captivity or captive bred in another state or nation.
PA.note: The prairie dog is named nowhere in Pennsylvania law. What arguably reaches it is this catch-all, which bars possessing wildlife captive bred in another state, read together with 34 Pa.C.S. § 102, where wild animals means every mammal except horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. That is the same reading the Game Commission uses to ban hedgehogs and sugar gliders, and it is an agency interpretation of a definition rather than a rule anyone wrote about this species. Recorded unclear rather than banned because no text names the animal.

MI.quote: badger, bobcat, red and gray fox, raccoon, coyote, beaver, otter, muskrat, mink, squirrels, striped skunk, woodchuck, opossum, ring-necked pheasant, bobwhite quail, Hungarian partridge, ducks, geese and wild turkeys
MI.note: Michigan's captive wildlife permit is a closed list of native game species and the prairie dog is not on it, nor is it native game here, so the permit regime does not reach it. The Large Carnivore Act covers only big cats and bears. Importing one calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection as a nonnative rodent under the MDARD rules.

GA.note: Georgia requires a wild animal licence for listed species, and the rodent entry on that list reaches the capybara. The Department of Natural Resources states on its own exotics page that listed species may not be held as pets, so in practice the licence is not a route for a pet.

DC.quote: no person shall keep any living member of the animal kingdom as a household pet except
DC.note: DC works from a closed list of seven permitted categories, one of which is domesticated rodents and rabbits. A capybara is a rodent but not a domesticated one, so it fits no category and is barred by default rather than by name.

NYC.quote: All large rodents (Rodentia), including ... prairie dog, capybara

FL.note: The prohibited list is reptiles only. Capybaras are kept in Florida under the state's captive wildlife framework rather than barred by this rule.

NY.note: Rodentia is outside the definition.

CT.quote: The felidae... the canidae... the ursidae... and the hominidae
CT.note: No rodent appears on the list, so size is not the test here the way it is in states that regulate by weight.

WA.quote: A person shall not own, possess, keep, harbor, bring into the state, or have custody or control of a potentially dangerous wild animal
WA.note: No rodent appears in the enumerated definition.

OH.note: No rodent appears on either Ohio list, so the capybara's size does not bring it in the way a snake's length would.

TX.quote: a person may not own, harbor, or have custody or control of a dangerous wild animal for any purpose unless the person holds a certificate of registration for that animal
TX.note: No rodent appears on the dangerous wild animal list, which is drawn by species rather than by size.

IL.quote: a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi
IL.note: No rodent appears on the closed list, so the capybara's size does not bring it in.

MN.quote: all members of the family Felidae except the domestic cat
MN.note: The regulated animal definition is cats, bears and non-human primates. No rodent appears in it.

NV.note: On neither list. Nevada does not state a default for unlisted species in the text read, so this does not resolve either way.

VA.note: Absent from the permit table despite being a rodent, because the table lists the rodents Virginia considers a release risk rather than the order as a whole.

MD.note: No rodent appears on the list, so Maryland's thirty pound weight test applies to cat hybrids rather than to size generally.

VT.quote: the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for the keeping or possession of any wild animal in captivity
VT.note: Same unresolved question as the prairie dog. The prohibition is broad and the permit route is closed by the regulation, but the text does not say whether captive bred stock of a non-native species is inside or outside it. Ask Fish and Wildlife rather than assuming.

DE.note: Caught by the same wild rodent wording as the prairie dog. Nothing in the rule carves out captive bred stock.

TN.note: Class III catch-all; not a native species, so Class II does not apply.

ID.quote: South American Rodents. All South American rodents except guinea pigs and chinchillas.
ID.note: Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris is a South American rodent and is not excepted.

KY.note: On neither restricted list. A transportation permit is required to import one.

RI.quote: no person shall be allowed to import, or possess any animals defined as exotic wild animals or native wild animals without first obtaining a permit from the Department
RI.note: Not domestic, not native, and not on the § 3.17 exempt list, so the general permit requirement applies. Private ownership permits are available for animals outside the order Carnivora.

NH.note: On neither the non-controlled list nor the controlled table. The Patagonian cavy is listed but the capybara is not, so there is no category that authorises a permit and no exemption either. Ask Fish and Game rather than assuming the silence means yes.

MO.note: A South American rodent, so not Missouri wildlife, and rodents are absent from the § 578.023 list.

KS.note: Outside the definition of a dangerous regulated animal.

SC.note: A rodent, and rodents appear nowhere in the list of wildlife needing an import permit.

MT.quote: "Domestic animal" means an animal that, through long association with humans, has been bred to a degree that has resulted in genetic changes... The term includes livestock, as defined in 81-2-702, dogs, cats, rodents, Eurasian ferrets, and poultry.
MT.note: The word rodents is written flatly into the domestic animal definition, which would put every rodent outside the exotic wildlife scheme. The substance of the definition is about animals bred into domestication, which a capybara plainly is not. Nothing classifies it either way.

AK.quote: The department may not issue a permit for the capture, possession, import, or export of any game animal... for use as a pet
AK.note: Not on the clean list.

SD.quote: A permit from the board is required to import nondomestic animals.
SD.note: A rodent, so outside the possession permit list, though the free entry permit applies to bringing one into the state.

AL.quote: Any of the following from any area outside the state of Alabama; ...species of skunk, wild rodent, or strain of wild turkey
AL.note: The largest rodent in the world, and a wild one. Nothing in the rule carves out captive bred stock.

IN.quote: A permit is required under this rule for the following Class I wild animals: (1) Rabbit (Sylvilagus floridanus). (2) Squirrel (Sciurus carolinensis, Sciurus niger, and Glaucomys volans).
IN.note: The only rodents in the rule are three Indiana squirrels.

ND.quote: "Nontraditional livestock" means any wildlife held in a cage, fence, enclosure, or other manmade means of confinement that limits its movement within definite boundaries
ND.note: Inside the nontraditional livestock definition, with no rule currently attaching a licence.

WY.quote: (v) All members of the order Rodentia from Africa;
WY.note: The rodent ban is geographic and reaches Africa only, so a South American rodent falls through to the discretionary permit at Section 13(d).

MS.note: No rodent appears on the list.

LA.note: Not among the listed animals.

OK.quote: The following wildlife species are exempt from import and export permits, commercial wildlife breeders licenses, noncommercial wildlife breeders licenses and commercial hunting area license requirements
OK.note: Absent from the exemption list, so a noncommercial wildlife breeder's licence and an import permit apply.

NE.quote: Importation: the following wildlife may be imported:
NE.note: The list clears the chinchilla, the degu, the gerbil, the guinea pig and the greater jerboa. The capybara is not among them.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: Not a bear, big cat, canid or primate, which with large snakes and crocodilians is the whole of the guidance.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: Not a canid, hyaenid, felid, ursid, rhino, elephant, primate or swine, which is the whole of the mammal half of the definition.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: Hydrochoerus is on no Hawaii list, so the default prohibition applies.

ME.note: Not on the rodent list, which stops at the brown rat in size terms.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: Not on the mammal list, which stops at the Norway rat and the chinchilla in rodent terms.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Capybaras - Hydrochoerus hydrochaeris, Hydrochoerus isthmus
UT.note: Controlled rather than prohibited, so a certificate of registration is required before collection, importation or possession, but a route exists. Same column as the bobcat and the two-toed sloth.

PA.quote: Game or wild held captive . Game or wildlife held in captivity or captive bred in another state or nation.
PA.note: The capybara is named nowhere in Pennsylvania law. What arguably reaches it is this catch-all, which bars possessing wildlife captive bred in another state, read together with 34 Pa.C.S. § 102, where wild animals means every mammal except horses, cattle, sheep, goats and pigs. That is the same reading the Game Commission uses to ban hedgehogs and sugar gliders, and it is an agency interpretation of a definition rather than a rule anyone wrote about this species. Recorded unclear rather than banned because no text names the animal.

MI.quote: badger, bobcat, red and gray fox, raccoon, coyote, beaver, otter, muskrat, mink, squirrels, striped skunk, woodchuck, opossum, ring-necked pheasant, bobwhite quail, Hungarian partridge, ducks, geese and wild turkeys
MI.note: Commonly reported as needing a Michigan DNR permit, and that is wrong. The permit to hold game in captivity covers the closed list of native species quoted here and authorizes captive-bred game only; a South American rodent is not game in Michigan and cannot be permitted under it because it is not eligible in the first place. No Michigan statute names the capybara. The live requirement is the certificate of veterinary inspection to bring one in as a nonnative rodent.

CA.quote: Family Canidae-All species (W)

GA.note: Order Carnivora, all species; only the ferret is excepted.

DC.quote: no person shall keep any living member of the animal kingdom as a household pet except
DC.note: None of the seven permitted categories covers a wild canid. DC bans by omission from a closed list, so nothing has to name the fennec fox.

NYC.quote: All dogs other than domesticated dogs (Canis familiaris), including ... dhole, fennec, raccoon dog

NY.quote: (with the exception of domesticated dogs and captive bred fennec foxes (vulpes zerda))
NY.note: Expressly carved out of the Canidae entry. Legal statewide, banned in NYC.

CT.quote: The canidae, including, but not limited to, the wolf, and coyote

AZ.quote: All species of the order Carnivora

OR.note: Non-wolf, non-indigenous Canidae, with the same closed permit route.

grandfathered.detail: ODA permits had to pre-date the 2009 Act.

WA.note: The Canidae entry covers wolves only.

OH.note: The canid entries are gray wolves and African wild dogs only.

TX.note: The canids listed are the coyote and jackal only.

IL.note: The canids listed are the wolf and coyote only.

MN.note: Canidae is absent from the definition entirely.

NV.quote: All species in the genera Vulpes, Fennecus
NV.note: Named twice over: the fennec fox is Vulpes zerda and the regulation also lists the older genus Fennecus.

MD.note: Caught by the bare word 'fox', with no genus qualifier and no exception for the fennec.

ID.quote: All Non-native Canidae Species.

IA.quote: A member of the family canidae of the order carnivora, including but not limited to wolves, coyotes, and jackals. However, a dangerous wild animal does not include a domestic dog.
IA.note: Vulpes zerda is a canid, and the only exception written into the paragraph is the domestic dog.

grandfathered.detail: Registration by 31 December 2007 was the only way in. No new route exists.

KY.quote: Fox (Genus Cerdocyon, Genus Lycalopex, Genus Otocyon, Genus Urocyon, and Genus Vulpes);
KY.note: Vulpes zerda falls in the last genus named. The section bars importing, transporting into Kentucky, and possessing.

RI.quote: no permits shall be granted by the Department to a private person authorizing the import, and/or possession of any exotic wild animals of the order Carnivora, or hybrids thereof, for which there is no USDA conditionally licensed or unconditionally licensed rabies vaccine
RI.note: Same closed door as the serval. Fennec foxes are canids with no licensed rabies vaccine.

NH.quote: 5   Fox, Gray; Fenec
NH.note: Exhibitor only, same as the serval. The table pairs the two common names under one row.

MO.quote: hyena, wolf, bear, nonhuman primate, coyote, any deadly, dangerous, or poisonous reptile
MO.note: Wolves and coyotes are named but foxes are not. Missouri's own red and gray foxes are separately barred from importation under 3 CSR 10-9, which does not reach the fennec.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: No canid appears anywhere in the definition.

SC.quote: a furbearer, a member of the family Cervidae, a nondomestic member of the families Suidae (pigs), Tayassuidae (peccaries), Bovidae (bison, mountain goat, mountain sheep), coyote, bear, or turkey (genus Meleagris). Furbearer includes, but is not limited to, red and gray fox, raccoon, opossum, muskrat, mink, skunk, otter, bobcat, weasel, and beaver;
SC.note: The furbearer list is open ended and names fox. Bringing one into South Carolina needs a Department of Natural Resources permit.

MT.quote: A person may not import into the state, possess, or sell any exotic wildlife unless: (a) the importation, possession, or sale of the exotic wildlife is allowed by law or commission rule
MT.note: No canid appears on the noncontrolled, controlled or prohibited list, so there is no rule allowing it. ARM 12.6.2225(4)(a) confirms the direction of travel: exotic wildlife may not be imported unless it has been classified.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals... The list may include, but not be limited to: ...(C) Canids;
WV.note: Canids are named as a category with no species detail, so a fennec fox is squarely within the guidance and squarely outside anything enforceable until the list exists.

AK.quote: The department may not issue a permit for the capture, possession, import, or export of any game animal... for use as a pet
AK.note: The only canid on the clean list is Canis familiaris.

SD.quote: (1) Of the order Carnivora, all nondomestic members of the following families: ...(b) Canidae;

AL.quote: Any of the following from any area outside the state of Alabama; any member of the family Cervidae (to include but not be limited to deer, elk, moose, caribou), species of coyote, species of fox, species of raccoon, species of skunk, wild rodent, or strain of wild turkey, black bear (Ursus americanus), mountain lion (Felis concolor), bobcat (Felis rufus), Pronghorn Antelope (Antelocapridae), any nondomestic member of the families Suidae (pigs), Tayassuidae (peccaries), or Bovidae (except bison).
AL.note: Species of fox, without qualification. Every fennec fox in the trade comes from outside Alabama, which is the trigger.

IN.quote: (3) Gray fox (Urocyon cinereoargenteus). (4) Red fox (Vulpes fulva).
IN.note: The two foxes on the Class II list are Indiana's own. Vulpes zerda is on none of the three lists, and 312 IAC 9-11-1 limits the permit requirement to animals referenced in the rule.

ND.quote: The board of animal health may require a license for nontraditional livestock maintained within this state.
ND.note: Same gap as the serval. Note that the statute bans skunks and raccoons outright and singles out wolves for tattooing, so foxes sit between the two and are named in neither.

WY.quote: A permit may be authorized upon approval for other warm-blooded wildlife unless otherwise specified in this regulation.
WY.note: Wyoming's prohibited list names the gray wolf, the red wolf and wolf hybrids but no fox.

MS.quote: Family Canidae: Genus Canis (wolves, jackals, and dingos; all species, including crosses between wolves and domestic animals); excluding coyote (Canis latrans); Chrysocyon brachyurus (maned wolf); Cuon alpinus (red dog or dhole); Lycaon pictus (African hunting dog);
MS.note: Four named canids plus the genus Canis. Vulpes zerda is none of them.

LA.quote: d. red wolf (Canis rufus); e. gray wolf (Canis lupus); f. wolf dog hybrid (Canis lupus or Canis rufus x Canis familiarus);
LA.note: The only canids listed are the two wolves and their dog hybrids.

OK.quote: (35) Fennec Fox.
OK.note: Named on its own line, separate from the dog entry, which exempts dogs except coyotes and native foxes. Oklahoma is one of the only states to clear the species by name.

NE.note: Vulpes zerda is within the genus named on the importation list. The separate captivity list at § 001.01B reaches Nebraska's own gray and red foxes, which need a Captive Wildlife Permit.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: No statewide rule reaches it. § 153A-131 hands the question to counties, several of which have used it.

VA.quote: Canidae   All Species   Wild Dogs, Wolves, Coyotes or Coyote hybrids, Jackals and Foxes
VA.note: Virginia restricts the whole dog family by name and spells out foxes in the common name column, so the fennec is caught by the same row as a jackal.

HI.note: Part A reaches the whole genus rather than naming the fennec, so Vulpes zerda is covered without appearing by name. Research and exhibition only.

ME.quote: Carnivora (Carnivores)   Mustela putorius furo   Domestic Ferret
ME.note: Maine's entire unrestricted carnivore list is one animal, the domestic ferret. Every other carnivore, the fennec included, needs a permit.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: The unrestricted mammal list has one carnivore, the European domestic ferret, plus wolf and dog hybrids. The fennec is on neither.

WI.note: Not a harmful wild animal under § 169.11(1)(a), which names only cougars, the bear family and wild or feral swine, and not on the NR 40 invasive list. Non-native species are exempt from captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). An animal brought in from out of state still needs a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Fennec fox - Vulpes zerda
UT.note: Controlled rather than prohibited, so a certificate of registration is required before collection, importation or possession, but a route exists. Same column as the bobcat and the two-toed sloth.

PA.quote: In the family Canidae . Species and subspecies of the coyote, the red and gray fox and a full-blooded wolf or crossbreed thereof not licensed by the Department of Agriculture.
PA.note: The Canidae line is species-specific and reaches only the coyote, the red fox, the gray fox and the wolf. The fennec fox is none of them. What arguably reaches it instead is the catch-all at § 137.1(a)(11) barring possession of wildlife captive bred in another state, since 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 makes every mammal but livestock a wild animal. Same agency interpretation that bans hedgehogs and sugar gliders, and no Pennsylvania text names the fennec fox, so this is recorded unclear rather than banned.

MI.quote: badger, bobcat, red and gray fox, raccoon, coyote, beaver, otter, muskrat, mink, squirrels, striped skunk, woodchuck, opossum, ring-necked pheasant, bobwhite quail, Hungarian partridge, ducks, geese and wild turkeys
MI.note: A neat illustration of how Michigan draws its line, because the permit list includes red and gray fox and the fennec fox is neither. Michigan regulates its own wildlife and leaves non-native exotics to the import rules, so a native red fox needs a permit to hold game in captivity and a fennec fox does not. The Large Carnivore Act reaches only the seven named cats and bears. Importing one calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection.

CA.quote: Family Felidae-All species (W)

GA.note: On the wild animal licence list under the cat family. Georgia DNR's position is that listed species may not be held as pets, and unlike the ferret and the sugar glider the serval has no carve-out written into the rule.

DC.quote: no person shall keep any living member of the animal kingdom as a household pet except
DC.note: The permitted list covers domesticated dogs and cats. A serval is neither, and there is no permit route in the section.

NYC.quote: All cats other than domesticated cats (Felis catus), including ... serval, caracal

NY.note: Felidae, with no applicable exception.

CT.quote: The felidae, including, but not limited to, the lion, leopard, cheetah, jaguar, ocelot, jaguarundi cat, puma, lynx and bobcat

grandfathered.detail: Primates under 35 lb imported before this date are exempt; the statute grandfathers by date generally.

AZ.quote: All species of the order Carnivora

OR.note: Non-indigenous Felidae. Permits had to pre-date the 2009 Act, so there is no route for a new animal.

grandfathered.detail: ODA permits had to pre-date the 2009 Act, so no new permit is available.

WA.note: The Felidae entry names eight big cats and the serval is not among them, so Washington is unusually permissive here.

grandfathered.detail: Lawful possession before 22 July 2007 is grandfathered.

OH.quote: Servals, excluding hybrids with domestic cats commonly known as savannah cats
OH.note: The serval itself is a dangerous wild animal; savannah cat hybrids are expressly carved out.

TX.quote: a lion; a tiger; an ocelot; a cougar; a leopard; a cheetah; a jaguar; a bobcat; a lynx; a serval; a caracal; a hyena; a bear; a coyote; a jackal; a baboon; a chimpanzee; an orangutan; a gorilla; or any hybrid
TX.note: Certificate of registration plus $100,000 liability insurance.

MI.note: Corrected from banned. The previous entry said the Large Carnivore Act covers servals, and it does not. The definition is a closed list of seven cats, and the serval, Leptailurus serval, is not among them; the drafters expanded leopard to snow leopard and clouded leopard and stopped there. Nothing else in Michigan reaches it: the captive game permit is a closed list of native species, and the Animal Industry Act bars only large carnivores and wolf-dog crosses by reference to their own acts. Importing one calls for a certificate of veterinary inspection. Local ordinance is the real constraint here, since Michigan municipalities may prohibit what the state allows and many ban exotic cats outright.
MI.quote: any of the following cats of the Felidae family, whether wild or captive bred, including a hybrid cross with such a cat: a lion, a leopard (including a snow leopard or clouded leopard), a jaguar, a tiger, a cougar, a panther, or a cheetah

IL.quote: a lion, tiger, leopard, ocelot, jaguar, cheetah, margay, mountain lion, lynx, bobcat, jaguarundi, bear, hyena, wolf or coyote
IL.note: The serval is NOT on the Illinois list, despite several secondary sources saying it is. Read the statute rather than the summaries here.

grandfathered.detail: Only if possessed on or before 1 January 2005 and brought into Animal Welfare Act compliance.

MN.quote: all members of the family Felidae except the domestic cat
MN.note: Minnesota bans the cat family wholesale with a single exception for Felis catus, so the serval is caught by the same words that catch a tiger. Possession has been unlawful since 2005 unless the animal was already held on 1 January of that year in compliance with the federal Animal Welfare Act.

NV.quote: All felines, except mountain lions and bobcats

VA.quote: Felidae   All Species   Cats*
VA.note: The table restricts the whole cat family by name rather than listing species, so the serval is caught by the same line as a lion. A special permit is required to import, possess or sell one.

grandfathered.detail: Cats carry the asterisk, so an animal held before 1 July 1992 and declared in writing by 1 January 1993 may be kept under a possession-only permit that renews every five years and cannot be transferred.

MD.quote: member of the cat family other than the domestic cat

NM.note: Likely Group IV as a dangerous species, but the list was not read, so this is not asserted.

TN.note: Class I is defined by example rather than by list, 'inherently dangerous to humans such as wolves, bears, lions', so whether a serval is caught turns on a judgement the statute does not make. Not resolvable from the text.

So this is neither cleared nor expressly banned, it is an application to DWR with no published answer. Worth noting the prohibited column's big cat entry lists Panthera, Acinonyx, Uncia and Puma by name under the federal Big Cat Public Safety Act, and the serval is not among them, so it falls to the unlisted default rather than the big cat ban.

The route out is the exotic wildlife possession permit under 34 Pa.C.S. § 2963 and 58 Pa. Code Ch. 147 Subchapter N, and it is written around facilities rather than pet homes: a separate permit for each animal, and a new applicant must document two years of hands-on work with the species at a recognized or approved facility, with a letter of reference from its owner or manager. The 2005 Joint State Government Commission report on exotic wildlife in Pennsylvania lists the serval among the lesser cats given minimum cage specifications, which confirms the Commission treats it as exotic wildlife rather than leaving it to the catch-all.

Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither the prohibited species list nor the inherently dangerous list. The only reptiles on either are gila monsters, beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, crocodilians and venomous snakes other than hognose.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians. Nothing here falls in those categories.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: Turtles are one of the seven permitted categories.

HI.note: Named on Part A, research and exhibition only.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Chelydra serpentina is native to eastern Wyoming, but the native-species trigger in Section 9(c) applies only to animals imported for commercial use, so captive-bred stock kept as a pet falls to the Section 10 catch-all. Taking one from the wild is a separate question governed by the nongame regulation referenced in Section 9(b).

MT.quote: "Exotic wildlife" means a wildlife species that is not native to Montana.
MT.note: The common snapping turtle is native to eastern Montana, which puts it outside the exotic wildlife lists entirely. Section 87-5-116 covers commercial taking of native reptiles, not private possession.

ME.note: Chelydra serpentina is native to Maine and does not appear on the list of unrestricted species, which is the ordinary pattern: the list is aimed at exotics and native wildlife is handled under the general permit requirement.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Additionally, persons may possess and hold captive fish, bullfrogs, mussels, aquatic turtles, alligators and other aquatic wildlife in compliance with Code Chapters 26.00, 27.00, 29.00, 30.00, 31.00, 32.00, 33.00, 34.00, 35.00, and Addenda Chapters I1.00, J1.00, and V1.00.
AR.note: The unrestricted list expressly hands aquatic turtles to a different set of chapters rather than answering for them, and the common snapping turtle is native to Arkansas and commercially harvested there. The answer exists, but not in this document.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Not a dangerous wild animal. Chelydra serpentina is native to Ohio and is a regulated species for taking and for commercial harvest under the Division of Wildlife's rules, which is a separate regime from Chapter 935 and worth checking before collecting one.

WA.quote: Class reptilia ... Order crocodilia, all species
WA.note: Not a potentially dangerous wild animal. The common snapping turtle is not native to Washington and has established in a few places after releases, which the department treats as an invasive problem rather than a possession one.

WI.quote: A person may possess a live native snapping turtle for the purpose of harvest authorized under s. NR 19.275 (4), 21.13 (4), or 22.13 (4) for no more than 7 days.
WI.note: Wisconsin treats the snapping turtle as a harvestable native rather than a pet. Collecting or possessing native turtles requires a small game hunting or fishing approval, and the recreated rule caps live possession at 7 days tied to an authorized harvest. Wisconsin repealed and recreated NR 16.12(3) effective 1 January 2027 (CR 25-092). Until then the rule allows taking or possessing up to 5 individuals of each non-listed native species. From that date possession of live native reptiles and amphibians is prohibited outright except under narrow exemptions, of which the one that matters to keepers is NR 16.12(3)(k): captive-bred colour variants acquired from a legal source. A wild-type native animal will no longer be keepable.

UT.cite: Utah DWR reptile and amphibian species tables, non-controlled non-native
UT.quote: Common snapping turtle - Chelydra serpentina
UT.note: Utah puts established non-natives in a deliberately permissive column: 'they may be collected or possessed in any number without a permit', precisely because the division treats them as problematic for native wildlife. Note the one-way rule that applies to every herp here, native or not: once removed from the wild it may not be released back.

PA.quote: Common snapping turtle ( Chelydra serpentina ) | July 1 to October 31 | 15 | 30
PA.note: The only turtle in the table with a real open season, and personal possession of up to 30 needs no permit. Three conditions bind. The animal has to be taken in season, taking requires a fishing license, and § 79.5 requires an annual permit before anyone may take, catch, kill or possess snapping turtles for sale, barter or trade. Then § 79.10(a) bars importing a native species from another jurisdiction, so a Pennsylvania snapping turtle has to come from your own lawful take rather than a seller in another state.

MI.quote: A fishing license is required to take amphibians and reptiles for personal use.
MI.note: Not protected, and the only turtle here with an open season. The conditions are specific: the season runs July 15 to September 15, the limit is two a day and four in total, and a fishing license is required to take one. Buying one is not an option, because reptiles and amphibians may not be bought, sold or offered for sale in Michigan, so a snapping turtle has to come from your own lawful take.

LA.note: Ambystoma is native to Louisiana, so taking one from the wild falls under the collecting rules rather than the nonnative lists. Captive bred stock is a different question the rule does not address directly.

KY.quote: Except as established in Section 5 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport into Kentucky, or possess the following exotic wildlife that are considered potentially injurious to native ecosystems:
KY.note: The only amphibians on either Kentucky list are the giant or cane toad and the African clawed frog. Ambystoma appears on neither, though the species is native to Kentucky so the native wildlife rules in 301 KAR 1 are a separate question.

WV.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means a mammal, bird, reptile, amphibian or aquatic animal, including a hybrid, that is dangerous to humans, other animals or the environment due to its inherent nature and capability to do significant harm.
WV.note: The definition can reach an amphibian in principle, but the categories the board is pointed at are bears, big cats, canids, primates, large constrictors, venomous snakes and crocodilians. A salamander is not plausibly any of them.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess, display, offer for sale, trade, barter, exchange, or adoption, or give as a household pet, any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following

HI.note: Conditionally approved, which is the opposite of what Hawaii's reputation would suggest. Part A restricts two other Ambystoma species, so the genus is split across two lists and the species name is what decides it.

WY.note: Wyoming adopts the federal injurious wildlife list wholesale, and 50 CFR 16.14 covers every species in the genus Ambystoma. That makes the tiger salamander one of the few animals Wyoming will not permit at all, and the ban follows from a federal disease rule about Batrachochytrium salamandrivorans rather than from anything Wyoming decided about salamanders.

MT.quote: "Exotic wildlife" means a wildlife species that is not native to Montana.
MT.note: Ambystoma tigrinum is native to Montana, so the exotic wildlife permit regime does not reach it at all. The only statute that singles out native amphibians is § 87-5-116, and that restricts taking them for commercial purposes rather than keeping one.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: The permit rule at 5 AAC 92.029 applies to live game, and the statutory definition of game stops at birds, reptiles and mammals. An amphibian is not game, so the strictest clean list in the country simply does not apply to it.

ME.quote: Amphibia (Amphibians)   Captive Bred Origin Only ... Anura (Frogs And Toads)
ME.note: Maine's amphibian section contains one order, Anura, and every entry in it is a frog or a toad. There is no Caudata order at all, so no salamander or newt of any species is unrestricted in Maine. The whole section is also limited to captive bred origin.
