VA.note: The permit table works family by family and contains no reptile relevant here. Virginia permits by table, so absence from it means no special permit applies.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: varanidae limited to water and crocodile monitors, helodermatidae, the venomous snake families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. Nothing here is among them.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only: carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants and primates. Reptiles fall under the Game, Fish and Parks rules instead, and a free entry permit still applies to importing any nondomestic animal.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state
LA.note: The prohibited and restricted nonnative lists name crocodilians, tegus, two monitors, the green iguana, several snakes and some frogs. No hognose is among them. Louisiana's only mention of Heterodon is the native eastern hog-nosed snake on its checklist of native species.

MO.quote: those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri
MO.note: Both the eastern and the western hognose are native to Missouri and neither is venomous for the purposes of the Class II list, so they fall in Class I.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Neither hognose is venomous for the purposes of Section 9(a), which is aimed at front-fanged species, and neither is on the Section 8 prohibited list. Both are native to Wyoming, so wild collection is governed separately from keeping captive-bred animals.

RI.quote: Snakes of the family Colubridae, as follows may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit: ... (xvi) Western Hognose Snake (Heterodon nasicus)
RI.note: Rhode Island is unusually precise here, and the two hognoses land on opposite sides. The western hognose is named on the no-permit list, while the eastern hog-nosed snake is treated as a native species whose possession as a pet is prohibited outright. Which hognose you are buying is the whole question.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: No hognose is native to Idaho. The rule's test is non-venomous or non-dangerous, phrased in the alternative, so even the rear-fanged mild toxicity that gets the hognose argued about elsewhere does not matter here: it clears on the second limb regardless.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: The clean list's only reptile test is venom. The hognose is rear-fanged with mild saliva toxicity and is not treated as a venomous snake, so it clears.

ME.note: Only the western hognose is named. The eastern hog-nosed snake is native to Maine and is not on the list, so which species you are buying decides the answer, the same split Rhode Island draws.

CA.quote: Family Colubridae-Colubrids: 1. Dispholidus typus (Boomslang) (D) 2. Genus Thelotornis (Bird, twig, or vine snakes) (D) 3. Genus Nerodia (watersnakes) (D)
CA.note: California restricts exactly three colubrid groups, two of them dangerously venomous rear-fanged African species and one, Nerodia, for invasiveness. Heterodon is on none of them.

OH.quote: "Restricted snake" means any of the following: (1) All of the following constricting snakes that are twelve feet or longer ... (2) Species of the following families: (a) Atractaspididae; (b) Elapidae; (c) Viperidae; (3) Boomslang snakes; (4) Twig snakes.
OH.note: The restricted snake list is three venomous families plus two named rear-fanged species plus eight large constrictors. The hognose is none of them. The eastern hognose is native to Ohio, so wild collection is a Division of Wildlife question.

WA.quote: Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus
WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang. The hognose is unaffected.

WI.quote: A person may take or possess up to 5 individuals or eggs of each species of native amphibian, lizard and snake that are not endangered or threatened
WI.note: The eastern hognose is a Wisconsin native, listed by DNR as Common rather than threatened, so it falls under the general native-herp cap rather than the endangered species rules. Wisconsin repealed and recreated NR 16.12(3) effective 1 January 2027 (CR 25-092). Until then the rule allows taking or possessing up to 5 individuals of each non-listed native species. From that date possession of live native reptiles and amphibians is prohibited outright except under narrow exemptions, of which the one that matters to keepers is NR 16.12(3)(k): captive-bred colour variants acquired from a legal source. A wild-type native animal will no longer be keepable.

PA.quote: Eastern Hog-nosed Snake ( Heterodon platirhinos ) | No open season | 0 | 0
PA.note: The condition is which hognose. The eastern hognose is Pennsylvania native, gets no open season and a zero limit, and cannot be imported from another jurisdiction under § 79.10(a), so it can be neither taken nor bought. The western hognose, Heterodon nasicus, which is what the pet trade almost always sells, is not on the Commission's native species list and so falls outside Chapter 79 entirely. Nearly every hognose in a Pennsylvania shop is lawful and the one in the field is not.

MI.quote: Reptiles and amphibians may not be bought, sold or offered for sale.
MI.note: The eastern hog-nosed snake is Michigan native and is not on the protected list, so it may be taken, but only on conditions. A fishing license is required, the limit is three a day and six in total across snakes, lizards and turtles combined, and the quoted sale ban means you cannot lawfully buy one in Michigan or sell the one you have. Personal collection is the only lawful route. The western hognose that dominates the pet trade is not a Michigan species at all, so it sits outside this order and is simply legal, which makes the answer depend entirely on which hognose is in the tank.

DC.quote: Captive-bred species of common cage birds, including chickens
DC.note: Captive-bred is doing real work here, and every African grey legally sold in the United States is captive-bred because the Wild Bird Conservation Act has barred commercial import of wild-caught birds since 1992.

HI.note: Named by binomial on the conditionally approved list.

FL.note: The prohibited list is reptiles only.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian. No bird appears in it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: The only bird needing an import permit is turkey of the genus Meleagris, and the pet trade exemption separately clears parrots.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No bird prohibition exists in the chapter. The only bird provision is a seven dollar annual licence fee for species the board requires to be licensed.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No bird is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Your county code is the operative layer.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: The permit-exempt list clears parrots, lovebirds, budgerigars, macaws and parakeets, excepting only the monk parakeet.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No bird category appears in the guidance at all.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No bird appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: Nondomestic birds are handled by ARSD 12:68:13 rather than the mammal permit list here.

VA.quote: Psittaciformes   Psittacidae   Myiopsitta monachus   Monk parakeet*
VA.note: The only parrot on the permit table is the monk parakeet. No other psittacine appears, so the African grey needs no state permit.

LA.quote: This commission regulation prohibits importation and private possession, and otherwise regulates certain wild quadrupeds, big exotic cats, and non-human primates as provided herein.
LA.note: The quadruped regulation reaches mammals only. No bird is listed.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds (including ring-necked pheasants and gray partridge) native to the continental United States
MO.note: The bird half of Class I is limited to species native to the continental United States. Psittacus erithacus is African.

WY.quote: Live warm-blooded wildlife listed in this section... may be imported, possessed or transported without a permit... (b) Birds: (i) Cage and aviary birds.
WY.note: Chapter 10 defines cage and aviary birds as exotic captive-reared birds such as parrots which are adapted to live and breed in a cage or would not survive in the wild in the state. An African grey is squarely within that, so no permit and no veterinary certificate are required by the Department.

NH.quote: A permit to import wildlife shall not be required for any person to import wildlife designated as non-controlled... (6) The following birds: ... c. Parrots (Psittaciformes)
NH.note: The non-controlled list names the whole order, so every parrot is covered. New Hampshire readopted this rule in April 2026, which makes it one of the most recently confirmed entries in the matrix.

RI.quote: Psittacidae (Parrots and their allies) except for Myiopsitta monachus (Monk Parakeet), which requires a permit
RI.note: The parrot family is permit-free with a single carve-out for the monk parakeet, which is the pattern in most states that regulate parrots at all.

MT.quote: The following noncontrolled exotic wildlife may not be released or transplanted in the state but may be possessed or sold as pets in Montana without a permit: (a) tropical and subtropical birds in the order Passeriformes, including but not limited to birds in the families: ... (xi) Psittacidae (parrots)
MT.note: Noncontrolled, so no permit is needed. The drafting is odd, since parrots are Psittaciformes rather than Passeriformes, but the family is named outright and the list is expressly not exhaustive.

ID.quote: non-poultry birds
ID.note: The bird category is drawn by exclusion rather than by listing families, so every parrot is a conventional pet. Idaho does not carve out the monk parakeet the way most states do.

AK.quote: Parrot, parakeet, cockatiel, macaw, and other members of the Family Psittacidae   not prohibited by federal or international law
AK.note: Psittacidae is on the clean list, but Alaska attaches a qualifier no other state does: not prohibited by federal or international law. That matters here, because the African grey was moved to CITES Appendix I in 2017. Appendix I bars commercial international trade rather than domestic keeping, so a captive-bred bird already in the country is fine, but paperwork is worth having.

ME.quote: Order Psittaciformes*   All Species in Order Psittaciformes (Parrots)   Except for: Myiopsitta monachus; Cyanoliseus patagonus; Enicognathus leptorhynchus; Enicognathus ferrugineus; Family Strigopidae
ME.note: The whole parrot order is cleared, but the asterisk carries the footnote that removes anything on CITES Appendix I or listed by the IUCN as Endangered. The African grey is both: it moved to Appendix I on 2 January 2017 and was assessed Endangered in 2016, months before this list was published. So the one parrot most people think of is outside the clearance while a macaw is inside it.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Congo African Grey Parrot, Timneh African Grey Parrot (Psittacus erithacus, P. timneh)
AR.note: Both greys are named individually, including the Timneh, which was split off as its own species in 2012. Arkansas is the useful contrast with Maine here: same bird, same CITES Appendix I status, and Arkansas simply names it while Maine's footnote strips it out.

CA.quote: Family Psittacidae-Parrots, Parakeets: Myiopsitta monachus (Monk or Quaker parakeet) (D)
CA.note: The only parrot California restricts is the monk parakeet. Every other psittacine, the African grey included, is outside section 671.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Birds are outside Chapter 935 entirely.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: Birds fall outside both the statute and the deleterious exotic wildlife rule.

WI.note: Meets Wisconsin's unregulated pet bird definition: psittacine, non-native, not federally endangered and not migratory. Only the monk parakeet is carved back out, by NR 40. Out-of-state birds need a DATCP import permit.

UT.quote: Parrots - Family Psittacidae - All species not native to North America
UT.note: Utah clears the whole parrot family by one line, provided the species is not native to North America. Unlike Wisconsin and a number of other states, Utah draws no monk parakeet carve-out, so the Quaker sits in the same noncontrolled column as the African grey and the cockatoo.

PA.quote: All migratory birds as defined in 50 CFR by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service of the Department of the Interior, game birds and any other birds designated by the commission, including, but not limited to, grouse, partridge, pheasant, quail and wild turkey.
PA.note: The Game Code reaches a bird only if it is a wild bird, and that definition is a closed set of three: federally listed migratory birds, game birds, and any other birds the Commission designates. The African grey is none of them. The Commission has used its designation power on exactly one pet parrot, the monk parakeet at 58 Pa. Code § 137.1(a)(9), which shows it designates by name rather than by category. Parrots are not covered as a group.

MI.quote: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is required for the import of exotic, circus and zoo animals, native wild animals, domestic rabbits, nonnative rodents, nonnative reptiles and amphibians, and non-poultry birds
MI.note: The African grey is named in no Michigan statute or order. The Large Carnivore Act covers cats and bears, the captive game permit covers native game, and the herp order covers reptiles and amphibians, so nothing reaches a pet parrot. The only requirement is the certificate of veterinary inspection for a non-poultry bird moved into the state.

DC.quote: a person shall not import into the District, possess... any living member of the animal kingdom, including those born or raised in captivity, except the following
DC.note: No invertebrate category exists in the permitted list, so every millipede, spider and scorpion is outside it. DC bans by omission rather than by name.

RI.quote: Nothing in this Part shall prohibit any person from possession of exotic animals or native animals of the class Insecta unless the animals of that class appear on the list of prohibited insects
RI.note: The blanket invertebrate exemption is written for the class Insecta. A millipede is a myriapod, so on the literal wording it stays inside the definition of exotic animal and needs a permit, exactly like the tarantula and the scorpion.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian. No invertebrate appears in it.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: The permit provision at § 50-16-20 lists furbearers, cervids, pigs, peccaries, bovids, coyote, bear and turkey. No invertebrate is in it, and Chapter 47-2 covers only big cats, bears and great apes.

ND.quote: A person may not keep a skunk or raccoon in captivity.
ND.note: No invertebrate appears anywhere in the chapter.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The definition names six cats, bears and non-native venomous snakes. No invertebrate is in it.

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: The only statewide statute covers venomous reptiles. Counties may regulate animals dangerous to persons or property under § 153A-131.

KY.quote: Except as established in Sections 5 and 6 of this administrative regulation, a person shall not import, transport, or possess the following inherently dangerous exotic wildlife:
KY.note: On neither Kentucky list, which are drawn around vertebrates and a few named pests.

WV.quote: Create a comprehensive list of dangerous wild animals, excluding wildlife, livestock and domestic animals as defined herein. The list may include, but not be limited to: (A) Bears; (B) Big cats; (C) Canids; (D) Primates; (E) Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes; and (F) Alligators and caimans;
WV.note: No invertebrate appears in the categories the board is directed to consider.

VA.quote: A special permit is required and may be issued by the department... to import, possess, or sell those nonnative (exotic) animals listed in the following table
VA.note: Absent from the permit table, which covers vertebrates.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles. No invertebrate appears.

SD.quote: a permit as described in § 12:68:18:03.03 is required to possess in South Dakota any nondomestic mammal, or any of its hybrids, listed in this section
SD.note: The possession permit list covers mammals only.

LA.quote: The following nonnative reptile and amphibian species are prohibited from importation, possession, sale, attempting to sell, transfer, release, and reproduction in the state
LA.note: No invertebrate appears in either of Louisiana's exotic animal rules.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds... and those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri.
MO.note: No invertebrate appears in any of the three wildlife classes.

HI.quote: Any animal that is not on the lists of conditionally approved, restricted, or prohibited animals shall be prohibited until the board's review and determination for placement on one of these lists
HI.note: No myriapod appears on any Hawaii list, so the default prohibition applies. Hawaii's concern with invertebrates is unusually close, given what introduced ones have already done to the islands.

WY.quote: "Cold-Blooded Wildlife" means all fish, amphibians, reptiles, mollusks, crustaceans...
WY.note: A myriapod is outside both chapters. Wyoming's silence here is structural rather than an oversight: the Game and Fish Commission's authority runs to wildlife as Title 23 defines it.

NH.quote: A permit to import wildlife shall be required for all species, including hybrids, designated as controlled as cited in Table 800.01.
NH.note: The prohibited invertebrate list is entirely aquatic and the controlled table has no invertebrate entries, so a millipede is unregulated here despite the broad definition of wildlife.

MT.quote: A person may not import into the state, possess, or sell any exotic wildlife unless: (a) the importation, possession, or sale of the exotic wildlife is allowed by law or commission rule
MT.note: Montana defines wildlife to end with the phrase or other wild animal, which reaches an invertebrate, and it runs a white list rather than a black list. The statutory noncontrolled list has no myriapod, and the commission's rule at ARM 12.6.2205 clears two scorpions and one hermit crab and nothing else. Absence is the answer here, and the answer is no.

ID.quote: No person may import into Idaho... possess or otherwise hold in captivity... any live wildlife, except those animals exempted by Idaho Code or these rules, without a corresponding... captive possession... license/permit from the Department.
ID.note: A millipede is animal life and is not on the conventional pets list, so the same literal reading applies. Idaho's deleterious exotic animal rules at IDAPA 02.04.27 do not mention myriapods either, so nothing prohibits one outright.

AK.quote: "game" means any species of bird, reptile, and mammal, including a feral domestic animal, found or introduced in the state, except domestic birds and mammals
AK.note: A myriapod is not game and needs no permit from Fish and Game.

ME.quote: Diplopoda (Millipedes) ... Spirostreptus gigas   Giant African Millipede
ME.note: Maine gives millipedes their own class section and names the giant African millipede twice, under Spirostreptus gigas and Mardonius parilis acuticonus. The species usually sold under that name today is Archispirostreptus gigas, which is the same animal under a later genus.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: The following species are exempt from Codes 09.02 (Possession Of Non-Native Wildlife In Captivity Restricted), 09.07 (Wildlife Breeder/Dealer Permit Required), and 09.10 (Wildlife Importation Permit Required)
AR.note: No myriapod is named, and the list's scope is birds, mammals, reptiles and snakes, so nothing here settles it.

CA.quote: (8) Class Crustacea   Crustaceans ... (9) Class Gastropoda   Slugs, Snails ... (10) Class Bivalvia   Bivalves
CA.note: No myriapod is restricted. Note that agricultural inspection at the state border is a separate regime from Fish and Wildlife's restricted species list.

OH.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following, including hybrids unless otherwise specified
OH.note: Outside Chapter 935 entirely.

WA.quote: "Potentially dangerous wild animal" means one of the following types of animals ... (a) Class mammalia ... (b) Class reptilia
WA.note: Not reached by RCW 16.30 or by the deleterious exotic wildlife rule.

WI.cite: Wis. Admin. Code ch. NR 40; Wis. Stat. § 169.04(4)(b)
WI.note: No invertebrate kept as a pet appears on NR 40, whose terrestrial invertebrate entries are forest and soil pests such as the emerald ash borer and jumping worm. Non-native species are outside captive wildlife licensing.

PA.quote: Wild birds, wild mammals and facsimiles thereof, regardless of classification, whether protected or unprotected, including any part, product, egg or offspring thereof, or the dead body or parts thereof (excluding fossils), whether or not included in a manufactured product or in a processed food product.
PA.note: The giant African millipede is neither a bird nor a mammal, so it is not wildlife and the Game Commission has no authority over it. The Fish and Boat Commission's Chapter 79 covers reptiles and amphibians. Pennsylvania's two animal agencies divide the field between them and a terrestrial invertebrate falls in the gap, so no state possession rule applies.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The giant African millipede is not a reptile or amphibian, so the herp order does not reach it, and it is not a cat, a bear or native game, so neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the captive game permit reaches it either. Michigan regulates terrestrial invertebrates through its invasive species list rather than any pet law, and no common pet invertebrate is on it.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Corn snake is not on the federal injurious wildlife list this rule points to.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: The clean list's only reptile test is venom.

AZ.note: Arizona's restricted live wildlife rule reaches crocodilians, elapids, burrowing asps, boomslangs, twig snakes, keelbacks and the brown tree snake. A common colubrid like the corn snake is not on it, and it is not an Arizona native, so no separate wild-collection rule applies either.

CA.note: California's restricted colubrid entries are boomslang, twig snakes and Nerodia. Corn snake is not California native, so the state's separate native-reptile take rules (Title 14 CCR §§ 40-43) don't reach it either.

CT.quote: The felidae... the canidae... the ursidae... and the hominidae
CT.note: The potentially dangerous animal list is entirely mammalian.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes

DE.quote: cobras, coral snakes, mambas, vipers, rattlesnakes, copperheads, cottonmouths, pythons, anacondas
DE.note: The banned list is venomous species plus pythons and anacondas by name. A corn snake is none of those.

FL.note: Not on FWC's prohibited/Reptiles of Concern list, which names large constrictors, monitors, tegus and the green iguana. Corn snake is Florida native, though, so this covers lawfully acquired possession only; wild take of the native population falls under FWC's separate nongame take and bag-limit rules, not checked in detail here.

GA.quote: The following list of species native to Georgia may not be held as a pet regardless of its origin or morphology.
GA.note: Corn snake is named on Georgia DNR's own list of native species that cannot be kept as pets, and the agency is explicit that captive-bred stock is treated the same as wild-caught: origin does not matter. This is a real blanket ban on a species commonly sold in pet stores elsewhere, grounded in Georgia's wild animal statute, O.C.G.A. § 27-5-4/27-5-5. We could not pin an exact numbered subrule beyond that statutory basis; the DNR guidance page is unambiguous regardless.

HI.note: Hawaii bans the entire snake suborder by name.

IA.note: The squamate half of Iowa's dangerous wild animal definition is exhaustively enumerated: monitors, helodermatids, the venomous families, and henophidia limited to reticulated pythons, anacondas and African rock pythons. A corn snake is in none of them.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians

IL.note: Illinois caps possession of native Illinois herptiles at 8 specimens total and 4 per species without a permit, and a sport fishing license is required to collect any native species from the wild. Corn snake is Illinois native. A $50 Herpetoculture Permit exempts a keeper from this possession cap. Boidae, by contrast, is specifically exempted from the whole permit process (relevant to rosy boa, not this species).

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

KS.quote: all non-native, venomous snakes.

KY.quote: Venomous exotic snakes of the families Viperidae, Atractaspididae, Elapidae, Hydrophidae, and Colubridae, except for hognose snakes (Genus Heterodon);
KY.note: The Colubridae entry on Kentucky's restricted list is limited to venomous rear-fanged colubrids. A corn snake is not venomous, so it was never inside the clause to begin with.

LA.note: Not among the individually-named restricted nonnative species (which include Boa constrictor by exact binomial). Corn snake is Louisiana native; we did not separately verify Louisiana's wild-take rules for the native population, only that ordinary possession of a lawfully acquired animal is not on the restricted list.

MD.note: Only Hydrophidae, Elapidae, Viperidae and Crotalidae are barred.

MN.quote: A snake, lizard, or salamander that is obtained from a permitted breeder or that was possessed before August 1, 2021, may be possessed as a pet.
MN.note: Since August 2021, Minnesota requires any pet snake to come from a permitted breeder (or be grandfathered from before that date). The rule is not limited to Minnesota-native species; it applies to snakes generally.

MS.note: The inherently dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(v) Colubridae (modern snakes);

NC.quote: It shall be unlawful for any person to own, possess, use, transport, or traffic in any venomous reptile that is not housed in a sturdy and secure enclosure.
NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic animal statute covers venomous reptiles. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captivity-prohibition chapter.

NE.note: Nebraska's captive wildlife rule exempts common non-dangerous exotic reptiles from its permit system; corn snakes are named as an example of a legal-to-own species in Game and Parks guidance. Corn snake is not Nebraska native.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;
NH.note: Corn snake is not New Hampshire native, so it falls cleanly within the general exotic-reptile allowance.

NJ.quote: A permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians, or nongame species not specifically exempted by Section 4.4.
NJ.note: We read New Jersey's exempted-species list directly: it names Boa constrictor, garter snakes and ribbon snakes among reptiles, but not corn snake. So a permit is required. Worth flagging clearly: New Jersey also lists the corn snake as a state Endangered species (its native range barely reaches southern NJ, and the wild population was decimated by habitat loss and poaching before an endangered listing in 1984). Per NJ Fish & Wildlife's own species account, "the collection or possession of wild corn snakes is prohibited by the New Jersey Endangered Species Act and is punishable with fines and/or imprisonment." A captive-bred, non-New Jersey-origin animal is a permit case under 7:25-4.5; a wild-collected New Jersey animal is a straight endangered-species violation, a much harsher regime.

PA.note: Note corrected. The one-per-species cap is right, but the previous entry read § 79.4 as a general permit requirement for continued possession regardless of origin. That section is a one-time grandfather permit for animals already held on January 1, 2007, and its application window closed on June 30, 2007. The rules that actually bind a milk snake today are § 79.10(a), which makes importing a native species from another jurisdiction unlawful, and § 79.9, which bars selling or buying a reptile taken from Pennsylvania and its progeny. Designated color morphs are exempt under § 79.12, which is how most captive-bred milk snakes are lawfully sold here.

SC.quote: eastern milksnakes reproduced in captivity and under 10 inches in total length are also permitted

TX.cite: TPWD Nonindigenous/Controlled Exotic Snake Permit rules
TX.note: Milk snake is not a controlled exotic snake or threatened species under TPWD rules. Several milk snake subspecies are Texas native; wild collection of native nongame wildlife generally requires a Texas hunting license, but a lawfully acquired pet-trade animal needs no TPWD permit.

UT.quote: Western milk snake, Lampropeltis gentilis: Limited possession (2 daily and yearly/4 total, per species)
UT.note: Utah's own species table names the state's native milk snake population "Lampropeltis gentilis" (a segregate now often split from the broader Lampropeltis triangulum complex commonly called "milk snake" in the pet trade) and caps daily/yearly take and total possession at a combined 4. The phrase "limited possession," not just "bag limit," suggests the cap is not purely about wild collection.

VA.note: No snake appears on Virginia's special permit table at all.

WA.quote: Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus
WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang.

WI.quote: A person may take or possess up to 5 individuals... of each species of native amphibian, lizard and snake that are not endangered or threatened.
WI.note: Milk snake is Wisconsin native. Wild possession/take is capped at 5 individuals under NR 16.12. More notably, our research found that "the purchase of native amphibians and reptiles is prohibited except as provided in specified exceptions," meaning simply buying a milk snake, even a captive-bred one, is restricted in Wisconsin because of its native status, unlike a non-native pet-trade species such as corn snake or ball python. Wisconsin repealed and recreated NR 16.12(3) effective 1 January 2027 (CR 25-092). Until then the rule allows taking or possessing up to 5 individuals of each non-listed native species. From that date possession of live native reptiles and amphibians is prohibited outright except under narrow exemptions, of which the one that matters to keepers is NR 16.12(3)(k): captive-bred colour variants acquired from a legal source. A wild-type native animal will no longer be keepable.

WV.quote: Constrictor snakes greater than six feet, and venomous snakes;
WV.note: A milk snake, at a couple feet, is nowhere near the six-foot constrictor threshold.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation

MI.quote: Reptiles and amphibians may not be bought, sold or offered for sale.
MI.note: The eastern milk snake is Michigan native and is not on the protected list, so it may be taken, but only on conditions. A fishing license is required, the limit is three a day and six in total across snakes, lizards and turtles combined, and the quoted sale ban means you cannot lawfully buy one in Michigan or sell the one you have. Personal collection is the only lawful route. Michigan protects the black rat snake and the eastern fox snake but not the milk snake, so this one stays on the takeable side of the line.

AL.quote: Any species of bird, mammal, fish, crustacea, mollusk, reptile, or amphibian listed as injurious wildlife under the Lacey Act (18 U.S.C. 42) from the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service;
AL.note: Rosy boa is not on the federal injurious wildlife list this rule points to, the same reasoning that clears the much larger boa constrictor here.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AZ.cite: AZGFD Commission Order 43 (Reptile and Amphibian Regulations)
AZ.note: Worth flagging clearly: rosy boa (listed by AZGFD as Lichanura trivirgata / L. roseofusca) is native to southern Arizona, and Commission Order 43 sets a wild-take and possession bag limit of 4 animals under a valid Arizona hunting license, since AZGFD treats it as a species of conservation concern. That licensing and bag-limit regime governs collecting one from the wild. It is separate from simply owning a captive-bred, pet-trade rosy boa, which is not on Arizona's restricted live wildlife list (R12-4-406, aimed at crocodilians, elapids and a handful of named dangerous colubrids) and needs no permit.

CA.note: Not on California's restricted species list, which names giant pythons and anacondas among constrictors, not small native boas. Worth flagging clearly, though: California's own native-reptile regulations (Title 14 CCR §§ 5.60 and 43) governing wild take and commercial captive propagation of native reptiles do not use the name "Lichanura trivirgata" at all. They instead name "Lichanura orcutti" (called "Northern three-lined boa" in the take-limit table), reflecting a genuine taxonomic split: genetic work in the early 2000s divided the rosy boa complex into two species, with California's own wild population now generally recognized as L. orcutti and L. trivirgata proper restricted to the southern end of the range (extreme southern CA/Baja/Sonora). Under § 5.60 a Californian may take up to 2 wild L. orcutti under a sportfishing license; under § 43 a native reptile propagation permit is required to commercially breed or sell them. None of this touches ordinary ownership of a captive-bred, pet-trade rosy boa (of either taxon), which remains unrestricted since it is not on § 671. The upshot: California treats its own wild boa population as a regulated native-take resource under a different scientific name than the common "rosy boa" pet-trade animal is usually sold under, which is exactly the kind of distinction a keeper could easily miss.
