AZ.note: Arizona's restricted-live-wildlife rule reaches the whole squirrel family by name (the same entry this site's prairie-dog research already documents), which covers the flying squirrel.

CA.note: Order Rodentia is restricted as a whole ('All species (D)') except for a specific list of domesticated species (hamsters, rats, mice, guinea pigs, chinchillas); flying squirrels are not among the exceptions. This section number is carried over from this site's prairie-dog research, which cites the same Sciuridae subsection for a different genus in the same family; the exact subsection should be re-confirmed against the primary text before publishing.

HI.quote: FAMILY Sciuridae Sciuridae (all in family, except the following two species for exhibition in government zoos only: Callosciurus prevosti (squirrel, prevost's) and Sciurus variegatoides (squirrel, variegated) and except all species in the genus Marmota for research in government universities only)
HI.note: Confirmed directly from the HDOA prohibited-animal-list PDF. The whole squirrel family is prohibited; the only carve-outs are two unrelated tree squirrels (zoo exhibition only) and marmots (university research only). The flying squirrel is not one of the named exceptions, so no legal pathway exists at all, unlike states where a science/exhibition permit at least exists.

VT.quote: the Commissioner shall not issue a permit for the keeping or possession of any wild animal in captivity
VT.note: Vermont bars bringing in, transporting, or possessing any live wild bird or animal without authorization, and permits are described as rarely issued outside science, education, or rehabilitation purposes.

UT.quote: Except as otherwise listed, all species are presumed prohibited. All species not listed will require an assessment before collection, importation, or possession will be authorized.
UT.note: Not listed anywhere in Table 3b-1, and the table's default is inverted: unlisted birds and mammals are 'presumed prohibited' and require a division assessment before possession will be authorized. So this is neither cleared nor expressly banned, it is an application to DWR with no published answer. The northern flying squirrel is also a Utah native, which brings the state's native wildlife rules to bear on a wild-caught animal independently of this table.

PA.quote: It is unlawful for a person to possess live wildlife taken from a wild state within this Commonwealth
PA.note: The southern flying squirrel is a Pennsylvania native wild mammal, so it is wildlife under 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 and both routes into a home are closed. Taking one here is barred by § 137.31(a), whose only exception is a permit to hold up to five foxes for urine collection. Buying one from out of state is barred by § 137.1(a)(11), which prohibits possessing wildlife captive bred in another state, and § 137.1(a)(10) covers wildlife taken alive from the wild. Unlike the small exotic mammals, this one does not rest on an agency reading of an open-ended definition. A native squirrel is squarely what the Game Code was written for.

MI.quote: badger, bobcat, red and gray fox, raccoon, coyote, beaver, otter, muskrat, mink, squirrels, striped skunk, woodchuck, opossum, ring-necked pheasant, bobwhite quail, Hungarian partridge, ducks, geese and wild turkeys
MI.note: Squirrels are on the closed list of species that may be held under a permit to hold game in captivity, so Michigan's native flying squirrel needs one. Two limits matter. The permit authorizes captive-bred game, so an animal taken from the wild cannot be brought under it, and the permit is issued for the species rather than as a general exotic pet licence. This is the opposite of the answer for the non-native rodents on this map, which need no permit at all.

CA.note: Varanidae is absent from section 671 entirely, so monitors of any size are unrestricted in California, the same finding already documented for the savannah monitor.

NY.quote: Asiatic (water) Monitor (Varanus salvator); Nile Monitor (Varanus niloticus); White Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis); Black Throat Monitor (Varanus albigularis ionides); Crocodile Monitor (Varanus salvadori); Komodo Dragon (Varanus komodoensis)
NY.note: New York's closed dangerous-wild-animal definition names six specific large monitors. Varanus acanthurus is absent.

MA.note: The only monitor lizard on Massachusetts's exemption list; it may be kept without a permit.

GA.note: The only monitor named on Georgia's licensed wild-animal list is Varanus niloticus (Nile monitor), restricted to scientific, educational or exhibition purposes. Varanus acanthurus is absent and so unrestricted.

TX.note: Monitor lizards do not appear on Texas's closed dangerous-wild-animal list, which is limited to named big cats, bears, canids and primates.

LA.note: Louisiana's prohibited nonnative-reptile list names the savannah monitor and Nile monitor specifically; Varanus acanthurus does not appear on either the prohibited or the restricted list. Louisiana is unusual in banning two monitors by name, but both are large species and the dwarf Ackie is not among them.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Monitor Lizards (Genus Varanus: V. acanthurus, V. albigularis, V. glauerti, V. jobiensis, V. kingorum, V. macraei, V. pilbarensis, V. prasinus, V. salvator, V. timorensis)
AR.note: Confirmed directly from the current AGFC PDF (revised 11/1/22). V. acanthurus is named outright on the unrestricted list.

VA.note: No monitor lizard, Varanus, or Varanidae entry appears anywhere in the nonnative-animal permit table.

KY.quote: Komodo dragon (Varanus komodoensis);
KY.note: The only monitor on the inherently-dangerous list is the Komodo dragon.

IA.quote: A member of the family varanidae, which are limited to water monitors and crocodile monitors.
IA.note: Varanus acanthurus is neither.

MT.quote: (xxiv) Varanidae (monitor lizard);
MT.note: The whole family is cleared as unregulated wildlife rather than restricted.

WA.quote: Family varanidae, only water monitors and crocodile monitors
WA.note: Washington restricts exactly two monitors, both reaching seven feet or more. The Ackie is not one of them.

OH.quote: (14) Komodo dragons
OH.note: Varanus komodoensis is named individually rather than the family being listed, so other monitors are outside the law.

WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;

MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so outside Class I, and well under the eight-foot dangerous-reptile registration threshold of § 578.023.

KS.note: Only non-native venomous snakes are named among reptiles.

SC.quote: 15. reptiles

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)

AL.note: Only tegus of the genus Salvator are named among the lizards.

IN.quote: (4) Venomous reptiles. (5) Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in the chapter or current administrative rules.

WY.quote: (i) Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation.

MS.note: The inherently-dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

OK.quote: monotypic species and subspecies of reptiles and amphibians not indigenous to Oklahoma are exempt from import and export requirements and commercial and noncommercial wildlife breeder's license

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute covers venomous reptiles, and does not ban even those. Everything else is a county question under § 153A-131.

SD.note: The possession-permit list covers mammals only; reptiles fall under Game, Fish and Parks rules instead.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: No lizard fits any of the seven permitted categories, the same finding already documented for the savannah monitor.

HI.note: Confirmed directly from the HDOA restricted-animal-list (Part A) PDF. Part A is headed FOR RESEARCH AND EXHIBITION; a university or licensed exhibitor can hold one by permit, but no pet permit path exists, the same treatment as the savannah and Nile monitor.

RI.quote: Possession of the Gila Monster, Beaded Lizard (Heloderatidae), and all Monitors (Varanidae) requires an exotic animal possession permit.

NJ.note: No Varanus or Varanidae entry appears on the exempt-species list; falls to the § 4.5 catch-all permit provision.

ME.note: Maine's clean list names only Varanus exanthematicus (savannah monitor) among monitors (documented in this site's savannah-monitor research). Varanus acanthurus is absent, so it falls back to Maine's general importation/possession permit requirement rather than the no-permit list. Whether an individual permit is actually issued for a pet Ackie was not separately confirmed.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The ackie monitor is Australian and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The ackie monitor is Australian and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: Alaska's clean list turns entirely on venom; a garter snake clears it the same way the hognose does.

AL.cite: Ala. Admin. Code r. 220-2-.92; ADCNR hunting & fishing regulations
AL.note: Alabama lets residents keep native, non-protected wildlife such as the garter snake within possession limits set by hunting and fishing regulations. A scientific collection permit is only required for species specifically protected as nongame.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.note: Arkansas's unrestricted list clears several New World colubrid genera by name (Lampropeltis, Pantherophis, Nerodia, and others), but every one of those entries excepts species native to Arkansas, and Thamnophis never appears on the list at all. As Arkansas's own native species, a garter snake isn't covered by the pet-trade clearance and instead needs the state's Permitted Captive Wildlife Species List.

AZ.note: Arizona bars an open season on a few rare native gartersnakes, the Mexican gartersnake and narrow-headed gartersnake, but the common garter snake isn't among them. Taking or handling one requires a valid AZ hunting/fishing license; simple possession of a lawfully-acquired one isn't separately restricted.

CA.quote: No common gartersnakes (Thamnophis sirtalis) may be taken in San Mateo, Los Angeles, Orange, Riverside, San Diego, and Ventura counties.
CA.note: Owning a garter snake is unrestricted; it is not on the Fish & Game Code § 671 restricted species list. Wild collection is a separate question: it requires a sportfishing license, carries a 2-per-day bag/possession limit, and is closed entirely in six Southern California counties where protected look-alike subspecies (including the endangered San Francisco garter snake) occur.

CO.note: Colorado's 'unregulated wildlife' category explicitly includes pet reptiles, and no license is required for private possession. Wild collection of Colorado's own native garter snakes falls under Chapter W-7 (Herpetofauna) instead.

CT.note: Falls outside all four of Connecticut's regulated wild-animal categories: Category One is four dangerous mammal families, Category Two is dangerous reptiles plus the monk parakeet, Category Three is native birds and amphibians, and Category Four is state-listed endangered/threatened/special-concern species. A common garter snake is on none of them.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: A garter snake fits this exemption from DC's general wild-animal ban squarely.

DE.cite: Del. Code tit. 7, c. 7; Del. Code tit. 3, c. 72
DE.note: Delaware's native-wildlife rules forbid keeping a Delaware-native reptile as a pet, and DNREC's own guidance is explicit that native wildlife isn't for private ownership. A narrow carve-out exists for a captive-bred, aberrantly-colored native snake held under permit, but an ordinary wild-type garter snake doesn't qualify.

FL.note: Not a reptile of concern; that list covers large invasive constrictors, monitors, and tegus. Florida's captive wildlife rule allows nonvenomous, unprotected reptiles to be kept as personal pets without a license.

GA.note: Georgia bars possession of nongame wildlife outside a short exempted list that names venomous snakes but not harmless native colubrids, so a garter snake doesn't qualify. Native-reptile permits under § 27-5-4 are issued only for scientific, educational, or exhibition purposes, not casual pet-keeping, and Georgia DNR's own guidance says this holds 'regardless of the origin or morphology' of the animal.

HI.note: Hawaii bans the entire snake suborder outright, with no exception for harmless mainland species. There is no permit path for a pet garter snake in Hawaii.

IA.quote: "Dangerous wild animal" means any of the following:
IA.note: The squamate half of the definition is exhaustively enumerated: monitors, helodermatids, the venomous snake families, and a short list of giant constrictors. A garter snake is none of them.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: Idaho's test is venom, not species or origin, so a garter snake clears the same way a hognose does.

IL.note: Illinois's Dangerous Animals Act is a closed list of big cats and never reaches ordinary colubrids. Illinois is a home-rule state, though, so a municipality can still restrict snake ownership on its own.

IN.quote: Wolves that are purebred. Bears (all species). Wild cats (all species)... Venomous reptiles. Crocodilians that are at least five (5) feet long.
IN.note: Indiana's Wild Animal Possession Permit reaches venomous reptiles and large crocodilians, not ordinary nonvenomous snakes. Wild collection of Indiana's own native reptiles and amphibians is capped separately at two per day and four per year per species, with a possession limit of four.

KS.quote: "Dangerous regulated animal" means a live or slaughtered parts of: (1) Lions, tigers, leopards, jaguars, cheetahs and mountain lions, or any hybrid thereof; (2) bears or any hybrid thereof; and (3) all non-native, venomous snakes.
KS.note: The only reptiles Kansas regulates are non-native venomous snakes.

KY.note: Kentucky's inherently-dangerous-wildlife list reaches Colubridae only when the snake is venomous. A garter snake isn't.

LA.note: Louisiana's prohibited nonnative reptile list is built around crocodilians, tegus, monitors, the green iguana, and a short list of large or venomous snakes; ordinary colubrids like the garter snake aren't on it.

MA.note: Named directly on the license-exemption list, so it may be kept without a permit under M.G.L. c. 131 § 23. Massachusetts works as an allow-list: only animals actually named on it are exempt, and this one is.

MD.cite: COMAR 08.03.09 (native reptile and amphibian regulations, adopted 1993)
MD.note: Maryland requires a permit to possess, breed, sell, or trade a species of reptile or amphibian native to the state, and the garter snake is a Maryland native.

ME.cite: Unrestricted Species list, Serpentes (Captive Bred Origin Only)
ME.note: Maine's unrestricted-species list runs through every North American colubrid genus commonly kept as a pet, kingsnakes, ratsnakes, hognose, watersnakes, and more, and Thamnophis is conspicuously absent from every entry. A Maine garter snake needs the state's separate captivity permit rather than falling under this pet-trade clearance.

MN.quote: all members of the family Felidae except the domestic cat
MN.note: Minnesota's regulated-animal statute reaches cats, bears, and non-human primates. No reptile appears in it.

MO.quote: those species of mammals... and nonvenomous reptiles and amphibians native to Missouri
MO.note: The garter snake is native to Missouri and nonvenomous, which places it in Class I, the tier that needs a simple possession permit rather than being unregulated.

MS.quote: Family Felidae: Genus Leo or Panthera or Neofelis (lions, tigers, jaguars, and leopards) - all species; Acinonyx iubatus (cheetah); Felis concolor (cougar) - all subspecies;
MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is entirely mammalian; no reptile is restricted at any size.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(v) Colubridae (modern snakes);
MT.note: Colubridae is cleared as nonvenomous, which covers a garter snake.

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute covers venomous reptiles. Everything else, including a garter snake, is left to county ordinance.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captive wildlife chapter.

NE.note: Nebraska allows residents to keep native, non-protected wildlife such as the garter snake within possession limits; the captivity ban in this rule targets wolves, skunks, and the cat and bear families, not common native reptiles.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;
NH.note: New Hampshire's noncontrolled reptile clearance turns on venom, not origin, so a garter snake is unaffected.

NJ.note: Not a potentially dangerous species; that list's only snakes are the venomous families (Elapidae, Viperidae, Crotalidae) plus boomslang, twig snakes, African kraits, and anaconda. A lawfully-acquired garter snake can be kept as a pet. Separately, New Jersey's own exotic-species guidance states plainly, 'It is illegal to take any animal from the wild,' so a wild-caught New Jersey garter snake is off the table even though owning one isn't.

NM.note: New Mexico's exotic wildlife rule sorts species into Groups I through IV by danger level; the garter snake isn't named in the regulation text located, and an unlisted species defaults to Group IV, whose actual permit requirements weren't confirmed in this research.

NV.note: Any reptile not classified as protected, sensitive, threatened, or endangered is unprotected in Nevada, and a common garter snake is not on any of those lists.

NY.quote: native snakes shall mean all life stages, including eggs, of the following species: ... common garter snake ... Open season: None.
NY.note: New York's 2006 native-herp law classifies the common garter snake as protected native wildlife with no open season, and DEC's own published guidance says the law 'does not differentiate between wild-caught and captive-bred animals.' DEC issues a possession permit for keeping a limited number of common native herp species, but that permit doesn't allow buying, selling, or breeding, so even a pet-store garter snake sits in a different legal category here than almost anywhere else.

OH.note: Ohio's restricted-snake list is three venomous families plus two named rear-fanged species plus large constrictors twelve feet and up. A garter snake is none of them.

OK.note: Non-indigenous reptiles are exempt from Oklahoma's import, breeder's-license, and permit requirements outright. Oklahoma's own native garter snake population instead falls under standard Wildlife Conservation hunting-license rules for wild take.

OR.quote: Milk, Pine, Corn, Rat, Garter snakes -- Colubridae -- All nonnative species except Boiga irregularis, Lampropeltis getula, L. zonata, and Pituophis catenifer
OR.note: Oregon's noncontrolled clearance for this group of colubrids is written for nonnative individuals. No equivalent express clearance was located for a garter snake that is an Oregon native, which instead appears to fall under the state's general nongame-wildlife holding-permit rule once three or more are kept.

PA.note: Corrected from legal. The common garter snake is Pennsylvania native and is not tabled by name, so the catch-all line caps possession at one animal. Two further rules bind that the previous entry missed. § 79.10(a) makes it unlawful to transport or import a native species into Pennsylvania from another jurisdiction, so an out-of-state garter snake is not an option, and § 79.9 bars selling or buying a reptile taken from Pennsylvania and its progeny. The designated color morphs at § 79.12 are the exception, exempt from the possession limit and sellable by registered propagators. Note that two Pennsylvania gartersnakes, the short-headed gartersnake and the eastern ribbonsnake, are tabled separately at zero.
PA.quote: Native species not listed in this subsection | No closed season | 1 | 1

RI.note: Rhode Island's exempt Colubridae list names sixteen groups of pet-trade snakes by genus, and Thamnophis is not one of them. The regulation states directly that possession of native snakes is restricted to institutions, meaning typical pet ownership of a Rhode Island garter snake isn't permitted.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only; reptiles fall under separate Game, Fish & Parks rules rather than this permit scheme.

TN.note: Tennessee's Class II covers native wildlife and requires a Wildlife Possession Permit with microchip or tattoo identification within 30 days. A garter snake, being Tennessee-native, falls in Class II rather than the unregistered Class III that non-native pet reptiles occupy.

TX.note: Texas's dangerous wild animal statute (Health & Safety Code ch. 822) is a closed list of big carnivores and doesn't reach ordinary snakes. Legal statewide, though some cities restrict snakes by ordinance.

UT.note: Non-controlled native reptiles, a category that includes garter snakes, may be possessed without a certificate of registration up to a threshold (three animals for most such species); holding more requires a certificate of registration from the Wildlife Board.

VA.note: Virginia's special-permit table works species by species and contains no reptile relevant to a garter snake.

VT.note: Vermont requires an Importation & Possession Permit for any wild animal not on its Unrestricted Wild Animals List. This research could not confirm whether the garter snake appears on that list.

WA.quote: Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus
WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang.

WI.note: Wisconsin lets residents possess up to five individuals of each non-protected native species, garter snakes included, without a permit, but native reptiles generally may not be bought or sold within the state, so a Wisconsin-kept pet has to come from your own lawful collecting rather than a breeder or shop. Wisconsin repealed and recreated NR 16.12(3) effective 1 January 2027 (CR 25-092). Until then the rule allows taking or possessing up to 5 individuals of each non-listed native species. From that date possession of live native reptiles and amphibians is prohibited outright except under narrow exemptions, of which the one that matters to keepers is NR 16.12(3)(k): captive-bred colour variants acquired from a legal source. A wild-type native animal will no longer be keepable.

WV.note: The only reptiles West Virginia's dangerous-wild-animal guidance points at are large constrictors, venomous snakes, and crocodilians.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Not venomous, and not on Wyoming's Section 8 prohibited list.

MI.quote: Reptiles and amphibians may not be bought, sold or offered for sale.
MI.note: The common garter snake is Michigan native and is not on the protected list, so it may be taken, but only on conditions. A fishing license is required, the limit is three a day and six in total across snakes, lizards and turtles combined, and the quoted sale ban means you cannot lawfully buy one in Michigan or sell the one you have. Personal collection is the only lawful route. Note that Butler's garter snake, a separate Michigan species, is on the protected list and may not be taken or possessed at all, so the answer turns on which garter snake you have.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: Alaska's clean list turns entirely on venom.

AL.note: Not native to Alabama, so it's an ordinary nonvenomous pet reptile rather than wildlife needing a possession-limit accounting; no restriction was found.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: New World Colubrid Snakes (in part) (Genera: Bogertophis, Drymarchon, Drymobius, Lampropeltis, Pantherophis, Phrynonax, Pituophis, Pseudelaphe, Senticolis, Spilotes) except species native to Arkansas
AR.note: Named on the unrestricted list by genus; the native-species exception in that entry doesn't reach the California kingsnake since it isn't an Arkansas species.

AZ.note: The California kingsnake's range reaches into parts of Arizona, so the same hunting/fishing-license framework that governs wild take of native reptiles applies there, but simple possession of a lawfully-acquired one isn't restricted, and it isn't on Arizona's no-open-season list.

CA.note: Not on the Fish & Game Code § 671 restricted species list, so owning one is unrestricted. Wild collection of a California kingsnake specifically requires a sportfishing license and is capped at a 4-per-day bag/possession limit; unlike the common garter snake, there are no county-level closures for this species.

CO.note: Colorado clears the genus Lampropeltis by name except for the western milksnake and the speckled kingsnake, neither of which is the California kingsnake.

CT.note: Outside all four of Connecticut's wild-animal categories, which reach only specific dangerous mammals, dangerous reptiles, native birds/amphibians, and state-listed species.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: A California kingsnake fits this exemption from DC's general wild-animal ban squarely.

DE.note: A live reptile not native to or generally found in Delaware needs a permit from the Department of Agriculture before it may be brought into the state, possessed, sold, or exhibited. The California kingsnake, a Pacific coast species, is exotic to Delaware.

FL.note: Not a reptile of concern; that category is built around large invasive constrictors, monitors, and tegus. Ordinary nonvenomous colubrids like the California kingsnake need no license as a personal pet.

GA.note: Georgia's wild-animal license rule doesn't name any snake at all, and the California kingsnake isn't Georgia native wildlife, so it falls outside both the wild-animal license scheme and the native-species possession restriction that reaches Georgia's own native kingsnake population.

HI.note: Hawaii's snake ban reaches every species in the suborder, kingsnakes included, with no pet-keeping permit available.

IA.note: The squamate half of Iowa's 'dangerous wild animal' definition is exhaustively enumerated (monitors, helodermatids, venomous families, a short list of giant constrictors); a kingsnake is none of them.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: Idaho's test is venom, not species.

IL.note: Illinois's Dangerous Animals Act is a closed list of big cats and never reaches ordinary colubrids. Illinois is a home-rule state, so a municipality can still restrict snake ownership on its own.

IN.note: Indiana's Wild Animal Possession Permit reaches venomous reptiles and large crocodilians, not ordinary nonvenomous snakes like a kingsnake.

KS.note: The only reptiles Kansas regulates are non-native venomous snakes.

KY.note: Kentucky's inherently-dangerous-wildlife list reaches Colubridae only when the snake is venomous.

LA.note: Louisiana's prohibited nonnative reptile list is built around crocodilians, tegus, monitors, the green iguana, and a short list of large or venomous snakes; ordinary colubrids like the kingsnake aren't on it.

MA.note: The whole genus is named on the license-exemption list, California kingsnake included.

MD.note: Not a Maryland native, so the state's native-reptile possession permit doesn't apply, and it's absent from the § 10-621 dangerous-animal list.

ME.cite: Unrestricted Species list, Serpentes (Captive Bred Origin Only)
ME.quote: All Species in Genus Lampropeltis (Kingsnakes And Milk Snakes) Except for: Lampropeltis herrerae; Lampropeltis triangulum triangulum
ME.note: The whole genus is cleared except two named species, neither of which is the California kingsnake.

MN.note: Minnesota's regulated-animal statute reaches cats, bears, and non-human primates. No reptile appears in it.

MO.note: Class I, Missouri's permit tier for nonvenomous reptiles, reaches only species native to Missouri. The California kingsnake isn't one, so it falls outside that requirement.

MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is entirely mammalian; no reptile is restricted at any size.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of nonvenomous snakes not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(v) Colubridae (modern snakes);
MT.note: Colubridae is cleared as nonvenomous.

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute covers venomous reptiles. Everything else is left to county ordinance.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captive wildlife chapter.

NE.note: Not endangered or threatened, and not one of the specifically prohibited carnivore families; an ordinary exotic pet reptile in Nebraska.

NH.quote: Reptiles, exotic, except: a. Alligator (Alligatoridae, spp); b. Crocodile (Crocodylidae, spp); and c. Venomous reptiles, other than the Western Hognose Snake;
NH.note: An exotic, nonvenomous reptile like the California kingsnake clears New Hampshire's noncontrolled list.

NJ.note: Absent from the potentially dangerous species table, which limits its snakes to venomous families plus boomslang, twig snakes, African kraits, and anaconda.

NM.note: New Mexico sorts exotic wildlife into Groups I through IV by danger level; the California kingsnake wasn't named in the regulation text located, and an unlisted species defaults to Group IV, whose actual requirements weren't confirmed in this research.

NV.note: Nevada's unprotected-reptile category covers most kingsnakes, though the state singles out California kingsnakes lacking a continuous banded/ringed pattern from head to vent as the specific unprotected form, so pattern can matter for certain individuals.

NY.note: New York's native-snake statute names its own indigenous species by common name, including the eastern milk snake (Lampropeltis triangulum); the California kingsnake is a Pacific coast species and isn't one of them, so it doesn't inherit the native-species possession permit that a New York garter snake needs. No other statute restricts it.

OH.note: Ohio's restricted-snake list is three venomous families plus two named rear-fanged species plus large constrictors twelve feet and up. A kingsnake is none of them.

OK.note: Non-indigenous reptiles are exempt from Oklahoma's import, breeder's-license, and permit requirements outright, and the California kingsnake isn't indigenous to Oklahoma.

OR.quote: Individuals of Lampropeltis getula, L. zonata and Pituophis catenifer that are morphologically distinct from native species.
OR.note: Oregon's kingsnake clearance, written under the older taxonomy in which the California kingsnake was classified as Lampropeltis getula californiae, only reaches individuals 'morphologically distinct from native species' -- in practice, a recognizable color or pattern morph rather than a wild-type-looking snake. Wild-caught, native-looking kingsnakes and their offspring aren't covered.

PA.note: Fish and Boat Commission possession rules apply only to species native to Pennsylvania. The California kingsnake isn't one, so it isn't reached by that chapter at all.

RI.quote: Kingsnakes and Milk Snakes
RI.note: Named directly on Rhode Island's exempt Colubridae list.

SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only; reptiles fall under separate Game, Fish & Parks rules.

TN.note: Not native to Tennessee, so a California kingsnake is Class III: a nonpoisonous, non-native reptile that needs no registration.

TX.note: Texas's dangerous wild animal statute doesn't reach ordinary snakes. Legal statewide, though some cities restrict snakes by ordinance.

UT.note: Falls under Utah's non-controlled reptile framework, the same one that clears the garter snake: up to three may be possessed without a certificate of registration, more with one from the Wildlife Board.

VA.note: Virginia's special-permit table works species by species and contains no reptile relevant to a kingsnake.

VT.note: Vermont requires an Importation & Possession Permit for any wild animal not on its Unrestricted Wild Animals List. This research could not confirm whether the California kingsnake appears on that list.

WA.quote: Family colubridae, only dispholidus typus
WA.note: The only colubrid Washington restricts is the boomslang.

WI.note: As a non-native species, the California kingsnake sits outside Wisconsin's native-reptile possession cap and can be kept the way corn snakes and ball pythons are, without a DNR license. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit and health paperwork.

WV.note: The only reptiles West Virginia's dangerous-wild-animal guidance points at are large constrictors, venomous snakes, and crocodilians.

WY.note: Not venomous, and not on Wyoming's Section 8 prohibited list.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The California kingsnake is a western species and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit. Michigan's native kingsnake relative is the eastern milk snake, which is covered; the California kingsnake is not.

AK.quote: Parrot, parakeet, cockatiel, macaw, and other members of the Family Psittacidae   not prohibited by federal or international law
AK.note: Cockatoos are on Alaska's clean list, but the 'not prohibited by federal or international law' qualifier matters: several cockatoo species, including the Moluccan and yellow-crested cockatoo, are CITES Appendix I, which bars commercial international trade even though it doesn't touch domestic keeping of an already-captive-bred bird.

AL.note: Parrots, cockatiels, conures, and macaws are generally legal in Alabama. Species listed under CITES or the Migratory Bird Treaty Act may need import/export paperwork, but that doesn't reach ordinary possession of a captive-bred bird.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Cockatoos: Lesser Sulphur-crested or Yellow-crested, Sulphur-crested, Umbrella or White, Salmon-crested or Moluccan, Goffin's (Cacatua sulphurea, C. galerita, C. alba, C. moluccensis, C. goffiniana)
AR.note: Five named cockatoo species, including two that are CITES Appendix I (yellow-crested and Moluccan), are on Arkansas's unrestricted list outright, a useful contrast with states like Maine that carve CITES-I birds back out of an otherwise blanket parrot clearance.

AZ.note: Most cockatoos are legal pets in Arizona; the state's live-wildlife statute (A.R.S. § 17-306) is aimed at native and dangerous wildlife rather than common cage birds.

CA.quote: Family Psittacidae-Parrots, Parakeets: Myiopsitta monachus (Monk or Quaker parakeet) (D)
CA.note: The only parrot California's restricted species list reaches is the monk parakeet. Every cockatoo species is outside section 671.

CO.note: Colorado's 'unregulated wildlife' category explicitly includes pet birds.

CT.note: The only psittacine Connecticut regulates under any of its four wild-animal categories is the monk parakeet. General parrots and cockatoos fall outside the regulation entirely.

DC.quote: Captive-bred species of common cage birds, including chickens
DC.note: Every cockatoo sold in the US pet trade is captive-bred, so this exemption from DC's general wild-animal ban applies the same way it does for the African grey parrot.

DE.note: Delaware exempts birds entirely from its exotic-animal permit system; only mammals and non-native reptiles are reached by that Title 3 permit requirement.

FL.note: Florida's prohibited/conditional captive wildlife lists are built around reptiles; no bird appears on them.

GA.note: Georgia's wild-animal license bird section names raptors and a handful of native passerines; it does not reach Psittaciformes at all.

HI.quote: White cockatoos (Umbrella, Moluccan, Sulphur-crested, Little Corella, etc.)
HI.note: Cockatoos are named on Hawaii's conditionally approved list, alongside the galah, gang-gang, black cockatoos, and palm cockatoo, so keeping one is possible but requires an import permit, pre-departure quarantine, health certification, and permanent ID before the bird ever lands in the state.

IA.note: Iowa's dangerous-wild-animal definition is drawn entirely around mammals and reptiles; no bird appears in it.

ID.quote: non-poultry birds
ID.note: Idaho's clean-list bird category is drawn by exclusion, not by naming families, so every parrot including cockatoos is a conventional pet.

IL.note: Illinois's Dangerous Animals Act is a closed list of big cats and doesn't reach birds. Illinois is a home-rule state, so a municipality could still restrict one.

IN.note: No bird appears in any of Indiana's three Wild Animal Possession Permit classes.

KS.note: Kansas regulates six big cats, bears, and non-native venomous snakes; no bird is in the definition.

KY.note: Kentucky's permit-exempt list clears parrots, lovebirds, budgerigars, macaws, and parakeets by name, excepting only the monk parakeet.

LA.note: Louisiana's quadruped regulation reaches mammals only; no bird is listed.

MA.note: Parrots are on Massachusetts's license-exemption list. This research could not confirm whether Massachusetts carves specific CITES Appendix I or IUCN-Endangered cockatoo species back out the way Maine's list does, so treat that narrower point as unverified even though ordinary cockatoo ownership is clear.

MD.note: Parrots, macaws, and cockatoos are legal in Maryland; they're outside both the § 10-621 dangerous-animal list and the Migratory Bird Treaty Act, which doesn't reach non-native species.

ME.quote: All Species in Order Psittaciformes (Parrots) Except for: Myiopsitta monachus; Cyanoliseus patagonus; Enicognathus leptorhynchus; Enicognathus ferrugineus; Family Strigopidae *Except if listed on: IUCN Red List (Endangered, Critically Endangered, or Extinct in the Wild) OR CITES Appendix I
ME.note: Maine clears the whole parrot order but then strips back out anything on CITES Appendix I or the IUCN's Endangered/Critically Endangered tiers. That carve-out catches several of the most commonly kept pet cockatoos: the Moluccan and yellow-crested cockatoos are CITES Appendix I, and the umbrella cockatoo is IUCN Endangered even though it's only CITES Appendix II. Smaller, more secure species like the cockatiel or galah would still clear the list; the larger, more iconic cockatoos generally need Maine's captivity permit instead.

MN.note: Minnesota's regulated-animal statute reaches cats, bears, and non-human primates; no bird is in it.

MO.quote: Class I wildlife shall include birds (including ring-necked pheasants and gray partridge) native to the continental United States
MO.note: The bird half of Missouri's Class I is limited to species native to the continental United States. No cockatoo is.

MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is entirely mammalian.

MT.quote: The following noncontrolled exotic wildlife may not be released or transplanted in the state but may be possessed or sold as pets in Montana without a permit: ...(xi) Psittacidae (parrots)
MT.note: Psittacidae is named outright on Montana's noncontrolled list, cockatoos included.

NC.note: No bird provision exists in North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute; it covers venomous reptiles.

ND.note: No bird prohibition exists in North Dakota's chapter beyond a modest annual license fee for species the board designates.

NE.quote: Cage and Aviary Birds - Means those captive-reared birds, not native to Nebraska, such as parrots, exotic finches, and canaries, which are adapted to live and breed in a cage.
NE.note: A cockatoo fits Nebraska's cage-and-aviary-bird definition; the one psittacine carved back out of that category is the monk parakeet.

NH.quote: Parrots (Psittaciformes)
NH.note: The whole order is named on New Hampshire's noncontrolled list.

NJ.quote: Psittaculis spp. – Ring-necked parakeets; Myiopsitta spp. – Monk (Quaker) parakeets; Cyanoliseus patagonus – Patagonian conures
NJ.note: New Jersey's potentially dangerous species table names exactly three psittacine groups, and Cacatua is not one of them.

NM.note: New Mexico sorts exotic wildlife into Groups I through IV by danger level; cockatoos weren't named in the regulation text located, and an unlisted species defaults to Group IV, whose actual requirements weren't confirmed in this research.

NV.note: Companion parrot species, cockatoos included, are not on Nevada's prohibited-species list and need no state permit.

NY.note: Cacatuidae does not appear on New York's Dangerous Animal License species list, which is built around big cats, bears, primates, and venomous reptiles. No New York statute or DEC regulation restricting parrot or cockatoo possession generally turned up in this research.

OH.note: Birds are outside Ohio's dangerous-wild-animal chapter entirely.

OK.note: Oklahoma's noncontrolled exotic-species exemption names cockatoos outright, along with cockatiels, macaws, canaries, and other psittacine birds.

PA.note: Conclusion unchanged, reasoning corrected. The previous entry said the Game Code does not reach birds at all, which is wrong: 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines wildlife as wild birds and wild mammals, and the Commission has designated the monk parakeet at 58 Pa. Code § 137.1(a)(9). The reason a cockatoo is lawful is narrower. Wild birds is a closed set of federally listed migratory birds, game birds, and birds the Commission designates, and no cockatoo is any of the three.
PA.quote: All migratory birds as defined in 50 CFR by the United States Fish and Wildlife Service of the Department of the Interior, game birds and any other birds designated by the commission, including, but not limited to, grouse, partridge, pheasant, quail and wild turkey.

RI.quote: Psittacidae (Parrots and their allies) except for Myiopsitta monachus (Monk Parakeet), which requires a permit
RI.note: The whole parrot family, cockatoos included, is permit-free with a single carve-out for the monk parakeet.

SC.note: The only bird South Carolina's import permit reaches is turkeys of genus Meleagris; the pet-trade exemption separately clears parrots.

SD.note: Nondomestic birds are handled by ARSD 12:68:13 rather than the mammal-only possession-permit list.

TN.note: A non-native cockatoo is Tennessee Class III: a nonpoisonous, non-native species that needs no registration.

TX.note: Texas's dangerous wild animal statute doesn't reach birds. Legal statewide, subject to local ordinance.

UT.quote: Parrots Family Psittacidae All species not native to North America
UT.note: Classified as noncontrolled, and a certificate of registration is not required to possess any noncontrolled bird.

VA.quote: Psittaciformes   Psittacidae   Myiopsitta monachus   Monk parakeet*
VA.note: The only parrot on Virginia's permit table is the monk parakeet.

VT.note: Vermont requires an Importation & Possession Permit for any wild animal not on its Unrestricted Wild Animals List. This research could not confirm whether cockatoos appear on that list.

WA.note: Birds fall outside both the potentially-dangerous-animal statute and the deleterious exotic wildlife rule.

WI.cite: Wis. Stat. § 169.04; DATCP pet bird rules
WI.note: A cockatoo meets Wisconsin's definition of an unregulated 'pet bird': psittacine, non-native, not federally endangered, not a migratory species. The one psittacine Wisconsin does prohibit is the monk parakeet, as an invasive species. Importing one from out of state still calls for a DATCP animal import permit and health certificate.

WV.note: No bird category appears in West Virginia's dangerous-wild-animal guidance at all.

WY.quote: Live warm-blooded wildlife listed in this section... may be imported, possessed or transported without a permit... (b) Birds: (i) Cage and aviary birds.
WY.note: Chapter 10 defines cage and aviary birds as exotic captive-reared birds such as parrots that are adapted to live in a cage; a cockatoo qualifies.

MI.quote: Certificate of Veterinary Inspection is required for the import of exotic, circus and zoo animals, native wild animals, domestic rabbits, nonnative rodents, nonnative reptiles and amphibians, and non-poultry birds
MI.note: Cockatoos is named in no Michigan statute or order. The Large Carnivore Act covers cats and bears, the captive game permit covers native game, and the herp order covers reptiles and amphibians, so nothing reaches a pet parrot. The only requirement is the certificate of veterinary inspection for a non-poultry bird moved into the state.

CA.note: Section 671's Testudines entries reach only Chelydridae (snapping turtles). No tortoise family is restricted, and California's own tortoise rules concern the native desert tortoise (Gopherus agassizii) as a protected species, not an exotic-possession restriction.

NY.note: No tortoise or Testudinidae entry appears anywhere in the closed dangerous-wild-animal definition, which among reptiles names only certain large monitors, big constrictors, venomous species and crocodilians.

MA.note: Massachusetts allows all species of turtles (up to 100 individuals/eggs per species) without a permit except five named exceptions: Argentina/Chaco tortoise, Gopherus spp. (gopher tortoises), pancake tortoise, spotted turtle, and red-eared slider. The red-footed tortoise is not among them.

NJ.note: Not on the exempt-species list (N.J.A.C. 7:25-4.4), which names only American anole, common iguana, boa constrictor, eastern painted turtle, snapping turtle, fence lizard, garter snake, tokay gecko and ribbon snake among reptiles. Falls to the § 4.5 catch-all: 'a permit shall be required for any other exotic mammals, birds, reptiles, or amphibians... not specifically exempted.'

VA.note: No tortoise, Chelonoidis, or Testudinidae entry appears in the nonnative-animal permit table. Subsection (H) allows possession of nonnative animals not listed in the table, subject to general law.

GA.note: Georgia's licensed wild-animal reptile list names only two turtles (African helmeted turtle, Chinese softshell turtle) under Order Testudines; no tortoise or Testudinidae entry appears.

DC.quote: Non-venomous snakes, fish, and turtles, traditionally kept in the home for pleasure rather than for commercial purposes
DC.note: A tortoise is a turtle in the taxonomic sense the category uses (Order Testudines), the same reading applied to the sulcata and Russian tortoise.

RI.quote: All exotic species of turtles may be kept without an exotic animal possession permit, except endangered species.
RI.note: The three tortoises pulled back out are the Chaco tortoise, the genus Gopherus and the pancake tortoise. Chelonoidis carbonarius is none of them and is not federally endangered.

FL.note: Not on Florida's prohibited reptile list (sixteen high-risk species, no tortoise) and not a Class I or II wildlife species requiring a specific license.

TX.note: Not on Texas's closed dangerous-wild-animal list (lions, tigers, and other named cats, bears, canids and primates). Tortoises and monitor lizards are outside the registration requirement.

LA.note: Absent from Louisiana's prohibited and restricted nonnative-reptile lists (which do name the savannah and Nile monitor). The native-turtle registration requirement at § 101.G governs Louisiana's own species and does not reach this South American tortoise.

MT.quote: all nonnative tropical and subtropical species of turtles with a carapace or shell length of more than 4 inches and not on the controlled or prohibited lists in the families: ...(ix) Testudinidae (tortoises);
MT.note: Cleared by family, above the four-inch floor, the same basis already used for the sulcata and Russian tortoise.

MS.note: Mississippi's inherently-dangerous list is drawn family by family and is entirely mammalian; no reptile is restricted under this rule at any size.

SC.quote: The importation of the following wildlife for sale in the pet trade does not require a permit: ...15. reptiles 16. amphibians.
SC.note: South Carolina exempts reptiles as a class from the import permit.

ND.note: No reptile appears anywhere in North Dakota's captive-wildlife chapter or current administrative rules.

KS.note: Kansas's only exotic-pet statute reaches six named cats, bears, and non-native venomous snakes. Tortoises are untouched at any size.

NC.note: North Carolina's only statewide exotic-animal statute covers venomous reptiles and does not ban even those. Everything else is left to county ordinance under § 153A-131.

KY.note: On neither the prohibited species list nor the inherently-dangerous list, which among reptiles names only gila monsters, beaded lizards, the Komodo dragon, crocodilians and venomous snakes other than hognose.

WV.note: The only reptiles the statute points the board at are constrictors over six feet, venomous snakes and crocodilians.

IA.note: The squamate/reptile half of Iowa's dangerous-wild-animal definition is exhaustively enumerated (certain monitors, helodermatids, venomous snakes, three named giant constrictors). No tortoise is among them.

SD.note: South Dakota's possession-permit list covers mammals only (carnivores, hoofed mammals, tapirs, rhinos, elephants, primates); reptiles fall under Game, Fish and Parks rules instead.

MO.note: Not native to Missouri, so outside Class I, and not a deadly or dangerous reptile over eight feet under § 578.023.

WY.quote: Amphibians and reptiles not listed in Section 8 or 9 of this regulation
WY.note: Non-venomous and not on the prohibited list, so no permit is required for personal use; the reptile must remain confined and never be released.

NH.quote: (4) Non-venomous reptiles, except the following: a. Indigenous reptile species listed in Table 800.1...
NH.note: No tortoise appears anywhere in the controlled table, so this non-native species clears the non-controlled category outright.

ID.quote: non-venomous or non-dangerous reptiles and amphibians
ID.note: A conventional pet under the reptile category, no size or weight qualifier attached.

AK.quote: Any nonvenomous reptile   Class Reptilia   (crocodile, alligator, snake, turtle, or lizard)
AK.note: No permit required; the clean list sets no size limit on reptiles.

OH.note: Not a dangerous wild animal and not native to Ohio, so nothing in Chapter 935 reaches it.

WA.quote: Class reptilia ... Order crocodilia, all species
WA.note: Not listed. Washington's reptile concerns under this chapter are venom and crocodilians rather than size or origin.

ME.note: Maine's own tortoise clearance list (documented in this site's sulcata-tortoise research) names the Russian, Greek, Hermann's, leopard, red-footed and yellow-footed tortoises by common name. The red-footed tortoise is expressly included; the exact binomial spelling used on Maine's PDF was not independently re-verified this round because the source PDF resisted text extraction, so double-check the primary document (maine.gov/ifw/docs/unrestrictedspecies.pdf) before publishing.

AR.cite: Code Addendum R1.01, Unrestricted Captive Wildlife Species List
AR.quote: Tortoises (Genera: Agrionemys, Aldabrachelys, Chelonoidis, Centrochelys, Geochelone, Gopherus, Indotestudo, Manouria, Psuedotestudo, Stigmochelys, Testudo)
AR.note: Confirmed directly from the current AGFC PDF (revised 11/1/22). Genus Chelonoidis is named outright, which covers the red-footed tortoise without ambiguity.

HI.cite: List of Conditionally Approved Animals, Family Testudinidae
HI.quote: Chelonoidis (all species in genus except C. elephantopus)
HI.note: Confirmed directly from the HDOA conditional-animal-list PDF. Unlike the sulcata (which moved out of Geochelone entirely into the unlisted genus Centrochelys, leaving its status genuinely unclear), the red-footed tortoise's current genus Chelonoidis is named outright on this list, with only the Galapagos tortoise (C. elephantopus, separately restricted) carved out. Chelonoidis carbonarius is squarely covered.

WI.note: Non-native, so it sits outside Wisconsin's native reptile possession rules in NR 16.12 and outside captive wildlife licensing under § 169.04(4)(b). Nothing in NR 40 reaches it. Bringing one in from out of state calls for a DATCP animal import permit.

PA.quote: A reptile or amphibian species or subspecies, where applicable, that has not been introduced into this Commonwealth and occurs historically within the boundaries of this Commonwealth.
PA.note: The red-footed tortoise is South American and does not appear on the Fish and Boat Commission's published list of Pennsylvania native species, so Chapter 79, which is built entirely around native species, does not reach it. Nothing else in Pennsylvania reaches it either. The Game and Wildlife Code applies to wildlife, which 34 Pa.C.S. § 102 defines as wild birds and wild mammals, so reptiles and amphibians sit entirely outside the Game Commission's exotic wildlife permit framework.

MI.quote: It shall be unlawful to kill, take, trap, possess, buy, sell, offer to buy or sell, barter, or attempt to take, trap, possess or barter any state reptile or amphibian from the wild
MI.note: The red-footed tortoise is South American and is not a Michigan reptile or amphibian, so the order that governs herps here does not reach it. Michigan's herp order reaches only a state reptile or amphibian taken from the wild, so a captive-bred non-native pet falls outside it, and neither the Large Carnivore Act nor the DNR's captive game permit reaches a reptile at all. Bringing one into Michigan needs a certificate of veterinary inspection under the MDARD import rules, which is a movement formality rather than a possession permit.
